atoms.title: Sets and functions
atoms.summary: A set is a collection of objects; a function is a rule assigning to each input exactly one output. These are the nouns and verbs of all modern mathematics.

depths.eli5: A set is just a bag of things — say, the numbers 1, 2, 3, or all the dots on a page. A function is a machine: you put one thing in (an 'input') and get exactly one thing out (an 'output'). It must never give two answers for the same input, and never refuse to answer. Squaring is a function: put in 3, always get 9.
depths.core: Almost every object in mathematics is built from sets (collections of objects), and almost every relationship between them is a function (a rule giving each input one output). The defining property is single-valuedness: each x in the input set, called the domain X, maps to exactly one y in the output set, called the codomain Y. Three words describe how a function behaves: injective (also called one-to-one) means no two different inputs share the same output; surjective (also called onto) means every possible output actually gets hit by some input; bijective means both at once — which is exactly the situation where the function can be run backwards (it has an inverse that undoes it).
depths.deep: Functions compose: do one then another and the result is itself a function, and this combining is associative (the grouping does not matter). That quiet fact makes 'sets and functions' an example of a category — the abstract stage on which limits, groups, and spaces are later defined. Cardinality — comparing the size of sets by whether you can pair their elements one-to-one (a bijection) — already defies intuition here: the whole numbers and the fractions turn out to be the same size, but the real numbers (every point on a continuous line) form a strictly bigger infinity.

atoms.note: Distinguish the function f (the whole machine) from its value f(x) (one specific output it produces). 'Domain' = the set of allowed inputs; 'codomain' = the set the outputs are drawn from.

quiz.prompt: What property must a relation between X and Y have to be a function, and what extra property makes it invertible?
quiz.answer: Each input maps to exactly one output (single-valued, total on X) to be a function; it is invertible exactly when it is bijective — both injective and surjective.

quiz.prompt: Is f(x) = x^2 from the reals to the reals injective? Surjective? How does restricting the codomain or domain change the answer?
quiz.answer: Not injective (x and -x collide) and not surjective onto all reals (negatives are never hit). Restrict the codomain to [0,∞) to make it surjective, and the domain to [0,∞) to make it injective; with both it becomes a bijection.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Before you can do *any* mathematics you need two things: a way to name **collections of objects**, and a way to describe **rules that turn one object into another**. A set is the collection; a function is the rule. Almost every later idea — numbers, groups, vector spaces, probability — is just a particular kind of set together with particular kinds of functions on it. Master these two and you have the grammar of the whole subject.

### Precisely
A **set** $X$ is an unordered collection of distinct objects called its **elements**; we write $x \in X$ for "$x$ is an element of $X$." A **function** $f\colon X \to Y$ assigns to *each* element $x$ of the **domain** $X$ *exactly one* element $f(x)$ of the **codomain** $Y$. Two demands are hidden in "exactly one": the rule must be **total** (every input gets an output) and **single-valued** (no input gets two outputs). Three adjectives describe behaviour: $f$ is **injective** ("one-to-one") if $f(a)=f(b)\Rightarrow a=b$; **surjective** ("onto") if every $y\in Y$ equals $f(x)$ for some $x$; and **bijective** if both — which is exactly when $f$ has an inverse $f^{-1}$ that undoes it.

### Worked example
Let $X=\{1,2,3\}$ and define $f(x)=x^2$ with codomain $Y=\{1,4,9\}$. Check the requirements: $f(1)=1,\ f(2)=4,\ f(3)=9$ — every input has one output (total, single-valued), so $f$ is a function. No two inputs collide, so it is injective; every element of $Y$ is hit, so it is surjective; hence $f$ is bijective with inverse $f^{-1}(1)=1,\ f^{-1}(4)=2,\ f^{-1}(9)=3$. Now change the codomain to all integers: $f$ is still injective but no longer surjective, because $7$ is never an output.

### Why it works
Functions **compose**: given $f\colon X\to Y$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$, the rule $(g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))$ is again a function, and composition is associative, $h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f$. A bijection is precisely a function you can run backwards, because single-valuedness in both directions is exactly what an inverse needs. This is why "invertible" and "bijective" mean the same thing.

### Where it connects
Single-valued composition that is associative is the seed of a **category** (`category-theory`). Comparing sets by whether a bijection exists between them defines **cardinality** (`set-theory-axioms`), where the surprise is that the rationals and the naturals match but the reals form a strictly larger infinity. Every algebraic structure later — `group`, `vector-space`, `ring-field` — is a set with chosen functions on it.

### Watch out
Do not confuse the function $f$ (the whole machine) with its value $f(x)$ (one output). And a function is not just a formula: it is the rule **together with** its domain and codomain. Changing either can flip whether $f$ is injective or surjective, as the example above shows.

atoms.title: Limits and continuity
atoms.summary: A limit pins down what value a function approaches; continuity is when that approached value equals the actual value. The epsilon–delta game makes 'approaches' precise.

depths.eli5: Imagine a function as a path. The 'limit' is the height the path is heading toward as you slide your finger toward a particular spot — even if the path has a hole right at that spot. The rule of the game: if a friend names any tiny target zone around that height, you can always get close enough on the input side to land inside it. If the height the path heads toward is the same as the height it actually has at the spot (no gap, no jump), the function is 'continuous' there — you could draw it without lifting your pen.
depths.core: The limit L is the number that f(x) can be forced arbitrarily close to (within any chosen tolerance written ε, the Greek letter epsilon) by keeping the input x within some small distance (written δ, delta) of a target point a — and you never actually need x to equal a. Continuity at a means the limit exists AND equals the real value f(a). The two Greek letters come from the standard 'epsilon–delta definition': ε is how close you must get to L, δ is how close you must stay to a to manage it. This single definition tames infinity by replacing vague 'gets close' talk with concrete, finite inequalities you can check.
depths.deep: The order of the quantifiers (the 'for all' / 'there exists' phrasing) is the whole subject: think of ε as chosen first by an opponent, and δ as your reply. Uniform continuity is a stronger version where one single δ must work everywhere at once, not retuned point by point. Completeness of the real numbers — the property that the number line has no missing points — is what guarantees the limits we expect actually exist: a 'Cauchy sequence' (terms that crowd ever closer together) is then guaranteed to converge to an actual number.

atoms.note: ε (epsilon, the required output closeness) comes first; δ (delta, the input closeness you supply) responds. Swap the order and you have instead defined uniform continuity.

quiz.prompt: In the epsilon–delta definition, who 'chooses' ε and who 'chooses' δ, and what does continuity at a add to the existence of the limit?
quiz.answer: The adversary fixes ε first; you must then produce a δ that works. Continuity at a additionally requires the limit to equal the function's actual value f(a).

quiz.prompt: Why is the function that is 0 on the rationals and 1 on the irrationals discontinuous at every point?
quiz.answer: Near any point both rationals and irrationals appear within any δ, so f takes both 0 and 1 arbitrarily close by; no single L can sit within ε < 1/2 of both, so the limit never exists.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A curve can *head toward* a value without ever reaching it — imagine a graph with a tiny hole punched in it. The **limit** captures the height the curve is aiming at, hole or no hole. **Continuity** is the happier situation where that aimed-at height is also the actual height: no gaps, no jumps, you could draw the graph without lifting your pen. The whole challenge is making the word "approaches" mean something a skeptic can check.

### Precisely
We say $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)=L$ when: for every tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a margin $\delta>0$ such that whenever $0<|x-a|<\delta$ we have $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. Read it as a game. An adversary names how close to $L$ you must land ($\varepsilon$); you must reply with how close to $a$ the input must stay ($\delta$) to guarantee it. The clause $0<|x-a|$ means $x=a$ itself is *excluded* — the value at $a$ is irrelevant to the limit. The function $f$ is **continuous at $a$** when the limit exists *and* equals the actual value: $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)$.

### Worked example
Take $f(x)=3x+1$ and show $\lim_{x\to 2}f(x)=7$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, we want $|3x+1-7|<\varepsilon$, i.e. $|3x-6|=3|x-2|<\varepsilon$, i.e. $|x-2|<\varepsilon/3$. So choosing $\delta=\varepsilon/3$ works: if $|x-2|<\delta$ then $|f(x)-7|=3|x-2|<3\delta=\varepsilon$. The reply $\delta$ depended on the challenge $\varepsilon$ — exactly the structure of the definition.

### Why it works
The genius is the **order of quantifiers**: "for all $\varepsilon$, there exists $\delta$." Because $\delta$ comes *after* $\varepsilon$, it may be retuned for each challenge. Swap the order — demand one $\delta$ that works for every point at once — and you have defined the stronger notion of **uniform continuity**.

### Where it connects
Limits are the foundation under the `derivative` (a limit of slopes) and the `integral` (a limit of sums). Continuity is generalized hugely by `metric-space` and `topology`, where "preimage of open is open" replaces $\varepsilon$–$\delta$. The guarantee that expected limits actually exist comes from **completeness** of $\mathbb{R}$ (`real-analysis`).

### Watch out
The value $f(a)$ does not affect the limit — a function with a hole can still have a perfectly good limit. The classic non-limit: the function that is $0$ on rationals and $1$ on irrationals has *no* limit anywhere, because every neighbourhood contains both kinds of point, so $f$ takes values $0$ and $1$ arbitrarily close, and no single $L$ can be within $\varepsilon<\tfrac12$ of both.

atoms.title: Groups
atoms.summary: A group is a set with one associative operation that has an identity and inverses. It is the minimal axiom system for 'symmetry' and 'reversible composition'.

depths.eli5: A group is a collection of 'moves' you can do and always undo. Doing two moves in a row counts as a single move, and there is a 'do nothing' move. Rotating a square by quarter-turns is a group; so is shuffling a deck. The point is just: combine moves, and you can always go back.
depths.core: Four rules (called axioms) define a group. (1) Closure: combining any two members gives another member. (2) Associativity: when you combine three, the way you group them — (a·b)·c versus a·(b·c) — does not change the result. (3) There is an identity element e, a 'do nothing' member that leaves others unchanged. (4) Every element has an inverse that combines with it to give e (an undo). These four rules capture a huge range of structures: whole numbers under addition, invertible matrices under multiplication, the symmetries of any shape. A group is called abelian (after mathematician Niels Abel) if the order never matters, i.e. a·b = b·a. The power: anything you prove from the axioms is instantly true for every group.
depths.deep: Groups 'act' on sets (they permute things), and the orbit–stabilizer theorem ties how many places an element can be moved to (its orbit) to the size of the subgroup that leaves it fixed (its stabilizer) — turning counting puzzles into algebra. Lagrange's theorem says the size of any subgroup must divide the size of the whole group, constraining structure before you know any details. The classification of finite simple groups — the 'periodic table' of basic symmetry building blocks — is one of the largest collaborative proofs in mathematics.

atoms.note: Associativity does quiet heavy lifting: it is what lets you write a·b·c with no parentheses. It fails for some operations (e.g. the vector cross product), which is exactly why those do not form groups.

atoms.art_prompt: a square with arrows showing its four rotational symmetries closing back on themselves as a cycle

quiz.prompt: Name the four group axioms.
quiz.answer: Closure under the operation, associativity, existence of an identity element, and existence of an inverse for every element.

quiz.prompt: Are the integers under multiplication a group? Why or why not?
quiz.answer: No — multiplication is associative with identity 1, but most integers (everything except ±1) lack a multiplicative inverse in the integers, so the inverse axiom fails.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A **group** is the mathematics of *reversible combining*. Think of a collection of "moves" — rotations of a square, shuffles of a deck, additions of whole numbers — where doing two moves in a row is itself a move, there is a "do nothing" move, and every move can be undone. Strip away everything specific and keep only those features, and you have isolated the pure structure of **symmetry**.

### Precisely
A group is a set $G$ with a binary operation $\cdot$ satisfying four axioms. **Closure:** $a\cdot b\in G$ for all $a,b$. **Associativity:** $(a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)$. **Identity:** there is an element $e$ with $e\cdot a=a\cdot e=a$ for all $a$. **Inverses:** each $a$ has an $a^{-1}$ with $a\cdot a^{-1}=a^{-1}\cdot a=e$. If additionally $a\cdot b=b\cdot a$ always, the group is **abelian** (commutative). Anything proved from these four axioms holds for *every* group at once.

### Worked example
The four rotations of a square — by $0^\circ,90^\circ,180^\circ,270^\circ$ — form a group under "do one then the other." Composition stays inside the set (closure); grouping does not matter (associativity); $0^\circ$ is the identity; and the inverse of $90^\circ$ is $270^\circ$ (together they make a full turn, i.e. the identity). It is abelian here because the order of two rotations does not change the result. By contrast, the integers under *multiplication* are **not** a group: $2$ has no integer inverse, since $1/2\notin\mathbb{Z}$.

### Why it works
Associativity quietly does the heavy lifting: it is exactly what lets you write $a\cdot b\cdot c$ with no parentheses. From the axioms one proves the identity is **unique** (if $e,e'$ both work then $e=e\cdot e'=e'$) and inverses are unique. **Lagrange's theorem** then says the size of any subgroup divides $|G|$ — structure forced by counting alone.

### Where it connects
Groups are the additive skeleton of `vector-space` and `ring-field`; structure-preserving maps between them are `homomorphism`s. Groups *act* on sets by permuting them, which links to `combinatorics`. Symmetry groups of equations drive Galois theory in `polynomials-roots`.

### Watch out
Not every operation is associative — the vector cross product is not — and such operations do **not** form groups. Also, closure is a real condition: a subset of a group can fail to be a subgroup simply because combining two of its elements escapes the subset.

atoms.title: The derivative
atoms.summary: The derivative is the best linear approximation to a function near a point — its instantaneous rate of change, and the slope of the tangent line.

depths.eli5: Pick a smooth curve and zoom in on one point. The closer you zoom, the more the curve looks like a straight line. The 'derivative' is the steepness (slope) of that line — it tells you how fast the output is changing right at that point, like a speedometer reading for the function. Going uphill steeply means a big derivative; flat means zero.
depths.core: The derivative f'(a) is built from the idea of average speed: take the change in output divided by the change in input over a small step h, namely [f(a+h) − f(a)] / h, then let the step h shrink toward zero (a 'limit'). The result is the instantaneous rate of change — the slope of the 'tangent line', the straight line just grazing the curve at that point. Equivalently it is the number m for which f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + m·h, with the leftover error shrinking faster than h itself. This 'local linearity' (a curve looks straight up close) is why calculus works: complicated curved behavior becomes locally straight, and straight is easy.
depths.deep: In more than one dimension the derivative is no longer a single number but a linear map (a matrix called the Jacobian) that best approximates the function near a point; differentiability means this approximation has error vanishing faster than the step size ‖h‖. The chain rule (how to differentiate a function of a function) then becomes simply 'multiply the linear maps'. Smoothness comes in a ladder: merely differentiable, then continuously differentiable (derivative itself continuous), then analytic (equal to its own power series) — and each rung is strictly stronger than the last.

atoms.note: Differentiable implies continuous, but not the reverse: the absolute-value function |x| is continuous at 0 yet has a sharp corner there, so it has no single slope — no derivative.

atoms.art_prompt: a curve with a tangent line touching it at one point, and an inset showing the curve and line nearly coinciding when zoomed

quiz.prompt: State the derivative as a limit, and say what geometric object it computes.
quiz.answer: f'(a) = lim_{h→0} [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h; it is the slope of the tangent line, the instantaneous rate of change at a.

quiz.prompt: Use the limit definition to show the derivative of f(x) = x^2 is 2x.
quiz.answer: [ (x+h)^2 − x^2 ]/h = (2xh + h^2)/h = 2x + h, and as h→0 this tends to 2x.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Zoom in on a smooth curve at one point and it starts to look like a straight line. The **derivative** is the slope of that line — the function's instantaneous rate of change, the reading on its speedometer at that instant. Steep uphill means a large positive derivative; flat means zero; downhill means negative. The entire power of calculus comes from this: complicated curved behaviour is, up close, just straight, and straight is easy.

### Precisely
The derivative of $f$ at $a$ is
$$f'(a)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},$$
when this limit exists. The fraction is the **average** rate of change over a step of size $h$ (rise over run); letting $h\to 0$ collapses the secant line through two nearby points into the **tangent line** at one point. Equivalently, $f'(a)$ is the unique number $m$ with $f(a+h)=f(a)+m\,h+o(h)$, where the error $o(h)$ shrinks faster than $h$ — the statement that $f$ is **locally linear** near $a$.

### Worked example
Differentiate $f(x)=x^2$ from the definition. Form the difference quotient:
$$\frac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h}=\frac{x^2+2xh+h^2-x^2}{h}=\frac{2xh+h^2}{h}=2x+h.$$
Now let $h\to 0$: the $h$ term vanishes, leaving $f'(x)=2x$. So at $x=3$ the slope is $6$.

### Why it works
The cancellation in the example is the whole mechanism: subtracting $f(a)$ removes the constant part, and dividing by $h$ exposes the linear part while the higher-order terms still carry a factor of $h$ that dies in the limit. This is why the derivative extracts precisely the *best linear approximation* and discards everything curvier.

### Where it connects
Stacking higher derivatives gives `taylor`'s polynomial approximations. Setting $f'=0$ locates extrema (`optimization`, `mean-value-theorems`). In several variables the single number becomes a matrix, the **Jacobian** (`multivariable-calculus`, `change-of-variables`). The derivative's inverse operation is the `integral`, tied together by the Fundamental Theorem.

### Watch out
**Differentiable implies continuous, but not conversely.** The function $|x|$ is continuous at $0$ yet has a sharp corner — the left slope is $-1$, the right slope is $+1$ — so no single tangent slope exists and $f'(0)$ is undefined. A derivative needs the curve to be *smooth*, not merely unbroken.

atoms.title: The integral and the Fundamental Theorem
atoms.summary: The integral accumulates a function over an interval as a limit of sums; the Fundamental Theorem makes integration and differentiation inverse operations.

depths.eli5: Want the area under a curve? Slice that area into a row of skinny rectangles, add up all their areas, then imagine making the slices thinner and thinner without limit — the running total settles on the exact area. That total is the 'integral'. The surprise (the Fundamental Theorem) is that this area is just the reverse of taking a derivative: if you know what you differentiated to get the curve, you get the area almost for free.
depths.core: The integral is an accumulation — it adds a function up across an interval. The Riemann integral (named after Bernhard Riemann) makes this precise: cover the area with rectangles, and the integral is the single value squeezed between the over-estimate and under-estimate as the rectangles get ever thinner (a 'limit' of sums). Its deep partner, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, has two faces: (1) differentiating an 'accumulation function' (area built up so far) gives back the original function you were integrating (the 'integrand'); (2) integrating a derivative returns the net change f(b) − f(a). This back-and-forth — integration undoes differentiation — is what turns calculus into a calculating machine: hard infinite sums get traded for 'antiderivatives' (functions whose derivative is the thing you want to integrate).
depths.deep: Riemann integration breaks down for very jagged functions and when you want to swap a limit with an integral. The Lebesgue integral fixes this by chopping up the range of outputs (the heights) instead of the domain of inputs (the widths), which buys the convergence theorems analysis depends on. The cost — and the reward — is measure theory, the rigorous study of how to assign sizes to sets.

atoms.note: The 'dx' is not decoration: it names the variable you are integrating over, carries the units, and is the piece that transforms when you change variables (substitution).

quiz.prompt: What two operations does the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus relate, and how?
quiz.answer: Differentiation and integration — it states they are inverse operations: d/dx of an accumulation of f returns f, and integrating f' over [a,b] returns f(b) − f(a).

quiz.prompt: Using the Fundamental Theorem, evaluate the integral of 2x from 0 to 3.
quiz.answer: An antiderivative of 2x is x^2, so the value is 3^2 − 0^2 = 9.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
You want the area under a curve. Slice it into thin vertical rectangles, add their areas, then make the slices ever thinner — the running total settles on the exact area. That limit is the **integral**. The astonishing payoff, the **Fundamental Theorem of Calculus**, is that this accumulation is the *reverse* of differentiation: if you know what you differentiated to get the curve, you get the area almost for free.

### Precisely
For a partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ into pieces of width $\Delta x_i$ with sample points $x_i^*$, the **Riemann integral** is
$$\int_a^b f=\lim_{\|P\|\to 0}\sum_i f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x_i,$$
the common limit of upper and lower rectangle sums as the mesh $\|P\|$ (widest piece) shrinks. The **Fundamental Theorem** has two halves: (1) if $F(x)=\int_a^x f$, then $F'(x)=f(x)$ — differentiating an accumulation returns the integrand; (2) if $F'=f$, then $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$ — integrating a derivative gives net change.

### Worked example
Compute $\int_0^3 2x\,dx$. By half (2) we need an **antiderivative** of $2x$ — a function whose derivative is $2x$. That is $F(x)=x^2$, since $(x^2)'=2x$. Then
$$\int_0^3 2x\,dx=F(3)-F(0)=3^2-0^2=9.$$
Check geometrically: the region under $y=2x$ from $0$ to $3$ is a triangle with base $3$ and height $6$, area $\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot6=9$. The slow limit-of-sums has been replaced by one subtraction.

### Why it works
Half (1) follows because $F(x+h)-F(x)$ is the area of a thin sliver of width $h$ and height $\approx f(x)$, so the difference quotient $\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}\to f(x)$. Half (2) then telescopes the accumulation back into a single difference. Differentiation and integration are genuinely inverse processes.

### Where it connects
The integral underlies `random-variables` (expectation is an integral), `fourier` analysis, `ode`, and `change-of-variables`. Its one-dimensional Fundamental Theorem is the simplest case of the `stokes-theorem`. For wilder functions it is upgraded to the Lebesgue integral (`measure-theory`).

### Watch out
The symbol $dx$ is not decoration: it names the integration variable, carries the units, and is what transforms under substitution. And Riemann integration fails for very jagged functions and when swapping a limit with an integral — situations that demand the Lebesgue theory.

atoms.title: Vector spaces
atoms.equation: u+v\in V,\quad \alpha v\in V,\quad \alpha(u+v)=\alpha u+\alpha v
atoms.summary: A vector space is a set where you can add elements and scale them by numbers, obeying distributive and associative rules. It is the arena of all of linear algebra.

depths.eli5: Picture a bunch of arrows starting from one spot. A vector space is a collection where you can (1) add two arrows by laying them tip-to-tail to get a new arrow, and (2) stretch or shrink any arrow by a number — and the result always stays inside the collection. That is it. Surprisingly, lists of numbers, polynomials, and even sound waves obey the same two rules, so they are vector spaces too.
depths.core: A vector space is a set whose members ('vectors') can be added together and multiplied by 'scalars' (numbers drawn from a field, such as the real numbers). Formally it is an abelian group under addition (so adding is commutative and reversible) plus a scalar multiplication that plays nicely with it, all pinned down by eight axioms. Those axioms guarantee a basis exists: a smallest possible set of vectors such that every vector is reached by exactly one 'linear combination' (sum of scaled basis vectors). The number of vectors in a basis is the dimension, and it completely classifies the space — every n-dimensional space over a given field is essentially just lists of n numbers.
depths.deep: The big leap is that a 'vector' need not be an arrow at all: the solutions of a linear differential equation, the polynomials of degree at most n, and the continuous functions on an interval are all vector spaces, so every theorem of linear algebra applies to them unchanged. When a space is infinite-dimensional you need extra structure from topology (a notion of size, called a norm, and completeness, meaning no missing limit points) for things to behave — that is where the subject called functional analysis begins.

atoms.note: Every subspace must contain the zero vector (the 'do-nothing' arrow at the origin). So a line that misses the origin is not a subspace.

atoms.art_prompt: two arrows from a common origin combining tip-to-tail into a third, with faint scaled copies of each

quiz.prompt: What is a basis of a vector space, and what does its size define?
quiz.answer: A linearly independent set that spans the space — every vector is a unique linear combination of it; its size is the dimension, a complete invariant of the space.

quiz.prompt: Is the set of polynomials of degree exactly 2 a vector space under the usual operations?
quiz.answer: No — it is not closed under addition (x^2 + (−x^2 + x) = x has degree 1) and lacks the zero polynomial; degree ≤ 2 is required to form a vector space.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A **vector space** is any world where two operations make sense and play nicely: you can **add** two objects to get a third, and **scale** an object by a number. Picture arrows from a common origin: add by laying them tip-to-tail, scale by stretching. The deep surprise is that lists of numbers, polynomials, sound waves, and solutions of linear equations all obey the *same* rules — so one theory governs them all.

### Precisely
A vector space over a field $\mathbb{F}$ (think $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$) is a set $V$ with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying eight axioms: $V$ is an **abelian group** under $+$ (associative, commutative, has a zero vector $\mathbf{0}$, has negatives), and scalar multiplication distributes over both kinds of addition, is associative ($\alpha(\beta v)=(\alpha\beta)v$), and has $1\cdot v=v$. A **basis** is a smallest set of vectors such that every vector is a *unique* **linear combination** $\sum \alpha_i v_i$ of them; the number of basis vectors is the **dimension**.

### Worked example
$\mathbb{R}^2$, the plane of pairs $(x,y)$, is the model. The standard basis is $e_1=(1,0),\,e_2=(0,1)$, and any vector splits uniquely: $(3,5)=3e_1+5e_2$, so $\dim\mathbb{R}^2=2$. Now consider polynomials of degree $\le 2$, $\{a+bx+cx^2\}$: add them coefficient-wise, scale them by constants, and the basis $\{1,x,x^2\}$ shows this is a *3-dimensional* vector space — even though its elements are functions, not arrows.

### Why it works
Once a basis is fixed, *every* vector is just its list of coordinates, so an $n$-dimensional space over $\mathbb{F}$ behaves exactly like $\mathbb{F}^n$. That is why dimension is a **complete invariant**: two finite-dimensional spaces over the same field are structurally identical precisely when they share a dimension.

### Where it connects
Maps between vector spaces that respect $+$ and scaling are `linear-map`s, encoded by matrices. Adding geometry (length, angle) gives `inner-product` spaces. Eigen-analysis (`eigenvalue`), `determinant`s, the `spectral-theorem`, and `svd` all live here. Infinite-dimensional spaces need topology (`metric-space`) and grow into functional analysis.

### Watch out
A **subspace** must contain $\mathbf{0}$ and be closed under both operations — so a line that misses the origin is *not* a subspace. And "degree exactly $2$" polynomials are not a vector space: they lack $\mathbf{0}$ and are not closed under addition (e.g. $x^2+(-x^2+x)=x$ has degree $1$). You need degree $\le 2$.

atoms.title: Linear maps and matrices
atoms.summary: A linear map preserves addition and scaling; once a basis is fixed it is encoded by a matrix, and composition of maps becomes matrix multiplication.

depths.eli5: Imagine graph paper. A linear map is a way of stretching, rotating, or shearing the whole sheet so that the grid lines stay straight and evenly spaced and the center point never moves. A 'matrix' is just the instruction sheet for that move: it records where each basic direction ends up, one column per direction. Multiplying matrices means doing one move after another.
depths.core: A linear map T is a transformation that respects the two vector-space operations: it sends a sum to the sum of the pieces and a scaled vector to the equally scaled result. Because of this, T is completely pinned down by where it sends the basis vectors (the chosen reference directions). Stacking those destination vectors as the columns of a grid of numbers produces the matrix. The rule (AB)v = A(Bv) is exactly why matrix multiplication is defined the way it is — it bookkeeps doing map B then map A. The rank–nullity theorem says: (input dimension) = rank + nullity, where the rank is how big the output (image) is and the nullity is how much gets crushed to zero (the kernel). So a map cannot both reach a lot and destroy a lot.
depths.deep: Switching to a different basis transforms the matrix by 'conjugation' with a change-of-basis matrix — meaning a matrix is just a coordinate-dependent shadow of a coordinate-free object. Quantities that survive that switch — rank, trace (sum of the diagonal), determinant, eigenvalues — are the map's genuine properties; the rest are artifacts of the coordinates you happened to pick.

atoms.note: Matrix multiplication is non-commutative (order matters): doing transformation A then B generally lands you somewhere different than B then A — like 'rotate then flip' versus 'flip then rotate'.

quiz.prompt: Why does fixing a basis let you represent any linear map as a matrix?
quiz.answer: Linearity means the map is determined by its action on the basis vectors; placing each basis vector's image as a column builds the matrix, and linearity reconstructs the map on all inputs.

quiz.prompt: State the rank–nullity theorem and say what it constrains.
quiz.answer: dim(domain) = rank(T) + nullity(T); the dimension of the image plus the dimension of the kernel equals the input dimension, so a map cannot both collapse a lot and reach a lot.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A **linear map** is a transformation of space that keeps grid lines straight, evenly spaced, and pinned at the origin — stretches, rotations, shears, but no bending and no shifting. A **matrix** is simply the instruction sheet for such a move: it records where each basic direction lands, one column per direction. Multiplying matrices means performing one move after another.

### Precisely
A map $T\colon V\to W$ between vector spaces is **linear** if $T(\alpha u+\beta v)=\alpha\,T(u)+\beta\,T(v)$ for all scalars $\alpha,\beta$ and vectors $u,v$. Because of this, $T$ is fully determined by its values on a basis: if $\{e_1,\dots,e_n\}$ is a basis of $V$, stacking the images $T(e_1),\dots,T(e_n)$ as columns produces the **matrix** of $T$. Matrix multiplication is *defined* so that $(AB)v=A(Bv)$ — it bookkeeps composition. The **rank–nullity theorem** states $\dim V=\operatorname{rank}(T)+\operatorname{nullity}(T)$, where rank is the dimension of the image and nullity is the dimension of the kernel $\{v: T(v)=\mathbf{0}\}$.

### Worked example
Let $T$ rotate the plane $90^\circ$ counterclockwise. It sends $e_1=(1,0)\mapsto(0,1)$ and $e_2=(0,1)\mapsto(-1,0)$. Place those images as columns:
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Check on $(3,5)$: $A(3,5)^{\mathsf T}=(0\cdot3-1\cdot5,\ 1\cdot3+0\cdot5)=(-5,3)$, exactly a quarter-turn. Linearity reconstructed the whole map from just two columns.

### Why it works
Linearity means $T\big(\sum x_i e_i\big)=\sum x_i\,T(e_i)$, so knowing the images of the basis determines $T$ everywhere — and arranging them as columns is exactly what makes matrix-times-vector compute the right answer. The rule $(AB)v=A(Bv)$ forces the otherwise-strange definition of matrix multiplication.

### Where it connects
Composition order matters: $AB\ne BA$ in general ("rotate then flip" $\ne$ "flip then rotate"). Invariants surviving a change of basis — rank, trace, `determinant`, `eigenvalue`s — are the map's true properties. This feeds `spectral-theorem`, `svd`, `ode` systems, and `orthogonality-least-squares`.

### Watch out
A matrix is a *coordinate-dependent shadow* of a coordinate-free map; change the basis and the numbers change while the underlying transformation does not. Rank–nullity also warns you: a map cannot both reach a lot (high rank) and crush a lot (high nullity) — they must sum to the input dimension.

atoms.title: Inner product spaces
atoms.summary: An inner product adds geometry — length and angle — to a vector space, defining orthogonality and enabling projection and best approximation.

depths.eli5: An inner product (the most common example is the 'dot product') is a recipe that takes two arrows and returns one number measuring how much they point the same way. If that number is zero, the arrows are at right angles. From this single number you can recover an arrow's length and the angle between two arrows — so geometry, which seemed like a separate subject, falls out of arithmetic.
depths.core: An inner product, written ⟨u,v⟩, is a rule for combining two vectors into a number that is symmetric (order does not matter), linear in each slot, and positive-definite (a vector dotted with itself is positive unless the vector is zero). From it you get a norm (length) ‖v‖ = √⟨v,v⟩ and an angle through cos θ = ⟨u,v⟩ / (‖u‖‖v‖). That angle formula only makes sense because the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality guarantees the ratio never exceeds 1. Two vectors are 'orthogonal' (perpendicular) when their inner product is zero. With an orthonormal basis (mutually perpendicular unit-length reference vectors), finding the closest point in a subspace becomes easy — just add up the projections onto each direction. That projection idea is the engine behind least-squares fitting and Fourier analysis.
depths.deep: When an inner product space is also complete (no missing limit points), it is called a Hilbert space; there, every closed subspace has a perpendicular complement and projections always exist. That one guarantee underwrites quantum mechanics — physical states are unit vectors and measurable quantities are 'self-adjoint' operators (ones equal to their own mirror-image transpose) — and equally underwrites signal processing.

atoms.note: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (|⟨u,v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖) is what makes 'angle' meaningful — without it, the cosine could come out larger than 1, which is impossible for a real angle.

quiz.prompt: What does an inner product add to a bare vector space, and what does ⟨u,v⟩ = 0 mean?
quiz.answer: It adds geometry — a notion of length (norm) and angle; ⟨u,v⟩ = 0 means the two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular).

quiz.prompt: State the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and explain why it guarantees a valid angle between two vectors.
quiz.answer: |⟨u,v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖; dividing gives |cos θ| = |⟨u,v⟩|/(‖u‖‖v‖) ≤ 1, so the ratio is a legitimate cosine and θ is well-defined.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A bare vector space lets you add and scale, but it cannot tell you a vector's **length** or the **angle** between two vectors. An **inner product** restores that geometry. Its most familiar form, the dot product, takes two arrows and returns a single number measuring how much they point the same way — zero meaning perpendicular. From this one number, length and angle reappear, so geometry turns out to be arithmetic in disguise.

### Precisely
An inner product $\langle u,v\rangle$ on a real vector space is **symmetric** ($\langle u,v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$), **linear in each slot**, and **positive-definite** ($\langle v,v\rangle>0$ unless $v=\mathbf 0$). From it come the **norm** $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ and the angle via $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\langle u,v\rangle}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}$. That formula is legitimate only because of the **Cauchy–Schwarz inequality** $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$, which keeps the cosine in $[-1,1]$. Vectors are **orthogonal** when $\langle u,v\rangle=0$.

### Worked example
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the dot product, take $u=(1,2,2)$ and $v=(2,0,-1)$. Then $\langle u,v\rangle=1\cdot2+2\cdot0+2\cdot(-1)=0$, so $u\perp v$. Lengths: $\|u\|=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3$, $\|v\|=\sqrt{4+0+1}=\sqrt5$. Cauchy–Schwarz says $|\langle u,v\rangle|=0\le 3\sqrt5$, comfortably satisfied, and indeed $\cos\theta=0$ confirms the right angle.

### Why it works
Positive-definiteness is what makes $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ a genuine length (never imaginary, zero only for $\mathbf0$). Cauchy–Schwarz can be proved by noting $\|u-tv\|^2\ge0$ for all $t$; the discriminant of this quadratic in $t$ being $\le 0$ yields exactly $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\|v\|$. With an **orthonormal basis** (perpendicular unit vectors), the nearest point in a subspace is found by summing projections onto each direction.

### Where it connects
Projection drives `orthogonality-least-squares` and the best-fit line. Orthogonal exponentials are the basis of `fourier` analysis. A complete inner product space is a **Hilbert space**, the arena of quantum mechanics and signal processing. The `spectral-theorem` lives here, where self-adjoint operators get orthonormal eigenbases.

### Watch out
Without Cauchy–Schwarz the "angle" could have $|\cos\theta|>1$, which is meaningless — so the inequality is not a technical footnote, it is what makes angle well-defined. Note too that different inner products give different geometries on the same space.

atoms.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
atoms.summary: An eigenvector is a direction a linear map only stretches, never rotates; its eigenvalue is the stretch factor. They expose the map's intrinsic axes.

depths.eli5: When you stretch or rotate a sheet of graph paper, most arrows get knocked off their original line. But a few special directions stay on their own line — they only get longer or shorter, never spun sideways. Those special directions are called eigenvectors, and the number telling you how much each one stretched (or shrank, or flipped) is its eigenvalue. ('Eigen' is German for 'own' or 'characteristic'.)
depths.core: An eigenvector v of a transformation A is a nonzero vector that A only scales: Av = λv, where the number λ (lambda) is the eigenvalue. To find the eigenvalues you solve the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0 — here det is the determinant and I is the identity matrix; this equation is a polynomial whose roots are exactly the eigenvalues. When a matrix has a full set of independent eigenvectors it is diagonalizable: rewritten in the basis of its eigenvectors, the transformation becomes plain multiplication by the eigenvalues, which makes raising the matrix to high powers (or exponentiating it) trivial.
depths.deep: Eigenvalues do not depend on the coordinate system, so they are true invariants of the operator, and they govern dynamics: the stability of equilibrium points, the growth or decay modes of linear differential-equation and recurrence systems, and resonance frequencies all read directly off the set of eigenvalues (the 'spectrum'). A 'defective' matrix that lacks enough eigenvectors needs the Jordan normal form, the structural patch to diagonalization.

atoms.note: A matrix with only real entries can still have complex eigenvalues. Those encode rotation: the size of the complex number is the scaling, and its angle is how much it rotates.
atoms.art_prompt: a transformed grid with two highlighted directions that stay on their own lines, one stretched and one shrunk

quiz.prompt: What geometric property distinguishes an eigenvector of A, and how do you find the eigenvalues?
quiz.answer: An eigenvector's direction is preserved by A (only scaled, not rotated); eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0.

quiz.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of the 2×2 matrix [[2,0],[0,3]] and explain why they are obvious here.
quiz.answer: It is diagonal, so det(A − λI) = (2−λ)(3−λ) = 0 gives λ = 2 and λ = 3; the standard basis vectors are already eigenvectors, scaled by 2 and 3.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Apply a linear transformation to space and most arrows get knocked off their original line — rotated, sheared, redirected. But a few special directions survive: they only get longer or shorter, never spun sideways. Those special directions are **eigenvectors**, and the factor by which each one is scaled is its **eigenvalue**. They reveal the transformation's own intrinsic axes — the skeleton hidden inside the matrix. ("Eigen" is German for "own.")

### Precisely
A nonzero vector $v$ is an **eigenvector** of a square matrix $A$ with **eigenvalue** $\lambda$ if
$$Av=\lambda v.$$
Rearranged, $(A-\lambda I)v=\mathbf0$ has a nonzero solution, which requires the matrix $A-\lambda I$ to be singular, i.e.
$$\det(A-\lambda I)=0.$$
This **characteristic equation** is a degree-$n$ polynomial in $\lambda$ whose roots are exactly the eigenvalues. If $A$ has a full set of $n$ independent eigenvectors it is **diagonalizable**: in the basis of eigenvectors it acts as plain coordinate-wise scaling.

### Worked example
Find the eigenvalues of $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $\det(A-\lambda I)=\det\begin{pmatrix}2-\lambda&1\\0&3-\lambda\end{pmatrix}=(2-\lambda)(3-\lambda)$. Setting this to zero gives $\lambda=2$ and $\lambda=3$. For $\lambda=2$, solve $(A-2I)v=0$: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}v=0$ forces the second coordinate to be $0$, so $v=(1,0)$ is an eigenvector — $A$ scales it by $2$.

### Why it works
The trick is that "$v$ keeps its direction" means $Av$ is a multiple of $v$, which is the equation $Av=\lambda v$. Demanding a *nonzero* such $v$ is exactly the condition that $A-\lambda I$ collapse some vector to zero, i.e. have zero determinant — turning a geometric question into a polynomial root-finding one.

### Where it connects
Diagonalization makes matrix powers and exponentials trivial, which solves linear `ode` systems and `recurrence-generating` relations: the dominant eigenvalue sets the growth rate. The `spectral-theorem` perfects this for symmetric matrices, and `svd` extends it to all matrices. Eigenvalues are coordinate-independent invariants, so they govern stability and resonance.

### Watch out
A real matrix can have **complex** eigenvalues — these encode rotation (modulus = scaling, argument = rotation angle). And a "defective" matrix lacking enough eigenvectors is *not* diagonalizable; it needs the Jordan normal form.

atoms.title: Taylor's theorem
atoms.summary: Taylor's theorem approximates a smooth function near a point by a polynomial built from its derivatives, with an explicit remainder bounding the error.

depths.eli5: Suppose you know exactly where a function is right now, how fast it is changing, how fast that change is changing, and so on. Taylor's theorem says you can then guess the function's value nearby by stacking up corrections: start with the value, add the slope times how far you moved, add a curvature term, then ever-finer wiggle terms. The more terms you keep, the better the guess — and there is an exact formula for how wrong you still are.
depths.core: A polynomial is a sum of powers like c0 + c1·x + c2·x² + … . Taylor's theorem builds the best degree-n polynomial approximation to a smooth function near a point a by matching the function's value and its first n derivatives there. The leftover error, called the remainder R_n, has an exact formula (the Lagrange form involves the (n+1)-th derivative at some point between a and x), so the approximation is a true equality, not a fudge, and the formula bounds how quickly accuracy fades as you move away from a. This is why linear approximation (keep 1 term) and quadratic models (keep 2) are everywhere in science — they are Taylor approximations with a known error budget.
depths.deep: If the remainder shrinks to zero as you keep adding terms (n → ∞) across a whole interval, the function exactly equals its infinite Taylor series there and is called analytic. Not every infinitely-differentiable ('smooth') function is analytic: the famous example e^(−1/x²) has every derivative equal to zero at the origin yet is not zero nearby, so its Taylor series at 0 is just 0 and misses the function entirely. That gap is one reason real analysis and complex analysis behave so differently.

atoms.note: A Taylor series can converge to a number that is NOT the function's value — convergence and equality are separate questions, and only the remainder term settles which you have.
atoms.art_prompt: a curve overlaid with progressively higher-degree polynomial approximations hugging it over a widening interval

quiz.prompt: What information about f at a point does the degree-n Taylor polynomial use, and what does the remainder term provide?
quiz.answer: The values of f and its first n derivatives at a; the remainder R_n gives the exact error, bounding how far the polynomial drifts from f away from a.

quiz.prompt: Write the degree-2 Taylor polynomial of e^x about 0 and use it to estimate e^{0.1}.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
If you know where a function is right now, how fast it is changing, how fast *that* is changing, and so on, you can predict its nearby values by stacking corrections: start with the value, add slope times distance moved, add a curvature term, then finer and finer wiggles. **Taylor's theorem** makes this exact, and — crucially — it tells you precisely how wrong any truncated guess still is.

### Precisely
For $f$ with $n+1$ derivatives near $a$,
$$f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k+R_n(x),$$
the degree-$n$ **Taylor polynomial** plus a **remainder** $R_n$. The polynomial is the unique degree-$n$ one matching $f$ and its first $n$ derivatives at $a$. The **Lagrange form** of the remainder is $R_n(x)=\dfrac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}$ for some $\xi$ between $a$ and $x$, so the formula is a true equality and bounds the error.

### Worked example
Approximate $e^{0.1}$ using the degree-$2$ Taylor polynomial of $e^x$ about $0$. Since every derivative of $e^x$ is $e^x$, valued $1$ at $0$, the polynomial is $1+x+\tfrac{x^2}{2}$. Plug in $x=0.1$:
$$1+0.1+\tfrac{0.01}{2}=1+0.1+0.005=1.105.$$
The true value is $1.10517\ldots$, so the error is about $1.7\times10^{-4}$ — and the Lagrange remainder $\tfrac{e^{\xi}}{6}(0.1)^3$ with $0<\xi<0.1$ confirms it is below $\tfrac{e^{0.1}}{6}(0.001)\approx 1.8\times10^{-4}$.

### Why it works
Matching $n$ derivatives forces the polynomial to agree with $f$ to $n$th order, so the first error term is governed by the *next* derivative — hence the $(n+1)$th derivative in the remainder. The factorial $k!$ appears because differentiating $(x-a)^k$ repeatedly produces it.

### Where it connects
Keeping one term is **linear approximation** (the `derivative`); two terms gives quadratic models used in `optimization`. Matching Taylor series proves **Euler's formula** in `complex-numbers`. If $R_n\to0$ on an interval, $f$ equals its infinite **Taylor series** there and is **analytic** — a property that becomes automatic in `complex-analysis`.

### Watch out
Convergence and equality are different questions. The function $e^{-1/x^2}$ (with value $0$ at $0$) has *every* derivative zero at the origin, so its Taylor series is identically $0$ — yet the function is not zero nearby. A Taylor series can converge to the wrong thing; only the remainder term settles whether the polynomial truly captures $f$.

atoms.title: Metric spaces
atoms.summary: A metric space abstracts 'distance', letting limits, continuity, and convergence be defined far beyond the real line. The triangle inequality is its load-bearing axiom.

depths.eli5: A 'metric' is any sensible way of measuring distance. It just has to obey common sense: a distance is never negative, the distance from A to B equals the distance from B to A, and going straight is never longer than taking a detour through some other point. Once you can measure distance, you can talk about points 'getting close' — and that lets the whole machinery of limits work not just on the number line, but on shapes, functions, even networks.
depths.core: A metric space is a set plus a distance function d obeying three axioms: (1) non-negativity, with distance zero only between identical points; (2) symmetry, d(x,y) = d(y,x); (3) the triangle inequality, d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,z) (no shortcut through a detour). From just these you can define 'open balls' (all points within some radius of a center), convergence, and continuity — so the same analysis runs on spaces of functions, spaces of sequences, and graphs, not only on the real numbers. Completeness — the property that every Cauchy sequence (terms crowding together) actually converges to a point in the space — is the extra ingredient that makes existence and fixed-point arguments safe.
depths.deep: The 'open sets' a metric produces generalize further into topology, where the idea of 'nearness' survives even when no distance is given. Compactness (every covering by open sets has a finite sub-covering) is the property that rescues the familiar power of 'closed and bounded' from the real line — it is what guarantees a continuous function attains a maximum, is uniformly continuous, and that sequences have convergent subsequences.

atoms.note: Two different metrics on the same set can produce the very same open sets (the same topology) — which means distance carries more information than mere nearness.
atoms.art_prompt: three points with edges labeled by distances, the direct edge visibly no longer than the two-edge detour

quiz.prompt: State the triangle inequality and explain why it is the crucial metric axiom.
quiz.answer: d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,z): a direct distance never exceeds a detour. It is what makes open balls and limits behave consistently, enabling continuity and convergence arguments.

quiz.prompt: What additional property must a metric space have for the Banach fixed-point (contraction mapping) theorem to apply, and why?
quiz.answer: Completeness — every Cauchy sequence must converge — so the iterates of the contraction, which form a Cauchy sequence, are guaranteed to have a limit point inside the space.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Almost everything analytic — limits, convergence, continuity — really only needs one ingredient: a notion of **distance**. A **metric space** abstracts exactly that. Once you can measure how far apart two things are, you can talk about them "getting close," and the whole machinery of calculus runs not just on the number line but on spaces of functions, spaces of sequences, even networks of cities.

### Precisely
A metric space is a set $X$ with a **distance function** $d\colon X\times X\to[0,\infty)$ obeying three axioms: (1) $d(x,y)\ge0$, with $d(x,y)=0$ iff $x=y$; (2) **symmetry** $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$; (3) the **triangle inequality** $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. From these come **open balls** $B(x,r)=\{y:d(x,y)<r\}$, convergence ($x_n\to x$ means $d(x_n,x)\to0$), and continuity. A space is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence (one whose terms crowd together) converges to a point in the space.

### Worked example
On $\mathbb{R}^2$ the usual (Euclidean) metric is $d\big((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)\big)=\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}$. Check the triangle inequality for the three points $A=(0,0)$, $B=(3,0)$, $C=(3,4)$: $d(A,C)=\sqrt{9+16}=5$, while the detour $d(A,B)+d(B,C)=3+4=7$. Indeed $5\le7$ — going straight is no longer than going via $B$. A different metric on the same set, the "taxicab" $d=|x_1-x_2|+|y_1-y_2|$, gives $d(A,C)=7$ but is still a valid metric.

### Why it works
The triangle inequality is the load-bearing axiom: it guarantees that if $x$ is near $y$ and $y$ is near $z$, then $x$ is near $z$ — the consistency that makes open balls nest sensibly and lets $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ continuity arguments transfer verbatim from $\mathbb{R}$ to any metric space.

### Where it connects
Metric spaces generalize the `limit` and continuity directly, and feed into `topology`, where "open set" survives even when no distance is given. **Completeness** powers the Banach fixed-point theorem (iterating a contraction converges), used to prove existence of solutions to `ode`s. **Compactness** rescues "closed and bounded."

### Watch out
Two different metrics can produce the *same* open sets (the same topology) — so distance carries strictly more information than mere nearness. Also, a metric space need not be complete: the rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ with the usual distance have Cauchy sequences (approaching $\sqrt2$) that converge to nothing inside $\mathbb{Q}$.

atoms.title: The spectral theorem
atoms.summary: Every self-adjoint operator has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues — it is diagonal in the right coordinates. This is the backbone of quantum mechanics and PCA.

depths.eli5: Some transformations are 'symmetric' — they look the same as their own mirror image. The spectral theorem says any such transformation has a set of mutually perpendicular axes along which it does nothing but stretch or shrink (by plain real numbers, never twisting). Switch your coordinates to those axes and the transformation becomes as simple as it could possibly be: just scaling.
depths.core: A 'self-adjoint' operator is one equal to its own conjugate-transpose, written A = A* (for a real matrix this means symmetric across the diagonal; for a complex matrix it is called Hermitian). The spectral theorem guarantees such an operator has all-real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis (perpendicular, unit-length eigenvectors). Consequently A splits into a sum of its eigenvalues times 'orthogonal projections' (operations that drop a vector onto one eigen-direction). Geometrically every self-adjoint map is pure stretching along perpendicular directions — no shear, no rotation, no defect.
depths.deep: This is precisely why measurable quantities ('observables') in quantum mechanics are modeled as self-adjoint operators: their real eigenvalues are the possible measured values and their perpendicular eigenstates are the distinguishable outcomes. The same theorem powers principal component analysis (PCA), which diagonalizes a covariance matrix to find the dominant directions in data, and the stability analysis of symmetric systems. The infinite-dimensional version, phrased with a 'spectral measure', is a cornerstone of functional analysis.

atoms.note: Self-adjointness is essential: a general matrix may not be diagonalizable at all, and a matrix that is 'normal' but not self-adjoint diagonalizes only if you allow complex numbers.
atoms.art_prompt: a symmetric transformation shown as pure stretching along three mutually perpendicular highlighted axes, no twisting

quiz.prompt: What does the spectral theorem guarantee for a self-adjoint operator?
quiz.answer: Real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors — equivalently, the operator is diagonalizable by an orthogonal/unitary change of basis into a sum of real eigenvalues times orthogonal projections.

quiz.prompt: Why must the eigenvalues of a quantum-mechanical observable be real, in terms of this theorem?
quiz.answer: Observables are modeled as self-adjoint operators, and the spectral theorem forces self-adjoint operators to have real eigenvalues — which is required because those eigenvalues are the physically measurable outcomes.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Some transformations are **symmetric** — they equal their own mirror image. The **spectral theorem** says any such transformation, however it may look, secretly does just one simple thing: it stretches space along a set of mutually perpendicular axes, by plain real factors, with no twisting at all. Rotate your coordinates onto those axes and the transformation becomes as simple as a transformation can be — pure scaling.

### Precisely
An operator $A$ on a real (or complex) inner product space is **self-adjoint** if $A=A^{*}$ — for a real matrix this means symmetric ($A=A^{\mathsf T}$); for complex, equal to its conjugate transpose (Hermitian). The theorem guarantees: all eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ are **real**, and there is an **orthonormal basis of eigenvectors**. Consequently
$$A=\sum_i \lambda_i P_i,\qquad P_iP_j=\delta_{ij}P_i,$$
where each $P_i$ is the orthogonal projection onto an eigen-direction. In one phrase: $A$ is diagonalizable by an orthogonal (unitary) change of basis.

### Worked example
Take the symmetric matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Its characteristic equation $\det(A-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)^2-1=0$ gives $\lambda=3$ and $\lambda=1$ — both real, as promised. The eigenvectors are $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ for $\lambda=3$ and $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ for $\lambda=1$; compute their dot product: $\tfrac12(1\cdot1+1\cdot(-1))=0$ — they are perpendicular. So $A$ is pure stretching: by $3$ along the $(1,1)$ diagonal and by $1$ along the $(1,-1)$ diagonal.

### Why it works
Self-adjointness forces eigenvalues real: if $Av=\lambda v$ then $\lambda\langle v,v\rangle=\langle Av,v\rangle=\langle v,Av\rangle=\overline\lambda\langle v,v\rangle$, so $\lambda=\overline\lambda$. It also forces eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues to be orthogonal, by a similar one-line computation. Together these give the perpendicular, real-scaling picture.

### Where it connects
This is *the* reason quantum-mechanical **observables** are self-adjoint: their real eigenvalues are the measurable values and their orthogonal eigenstates the distinguishable outcomes. It powers **principal component analysis** (diagonalizing a covariance matrix) and is the symmetric special case behind `svd`. It builds on `eigenvalue` and `inner-product`.

### Watch out
Self-adjointness is essential. A general matrix may not be diagonalizable at all, and a "normal" but non-self-adjoint matrix diagonalizes only over the complex numbers and with complex eigenvalues. Symmetry is what guarantees the clean real, orthogonal picture.

atoms.title: The generalized Stokes' theorem
atoms.summary: The integral of a differential form over a boundary equals the integral of its derivative over the interior. One identity unifies the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's, Gauss's, and the classical Stokes' theorems.

depths.eli5: Here is one big idea that secretly contains several famous calculus theorems: whatever a quantity does on the edge (boundary) of a region equals the total of what its 'derivative' does throughout the inside. If you imagine the inside chopped into tiny cells, each cell's swirl or flow is shared with its neighbors and cancels — only the outermost edge survives. So edge behavior = sum of interior behavior.
depths.core: The clean statement uses 'differential forms' — objects designed to be integrated over curves, surfaces, and higher-dimensional regions, with an operation called the exterior derivative, written d. The generalized Stokes' theorem says: the integral of dω over a region Ω equals the integral of ω over that region's boundary ∂Ω (the symbol ∂ means 'boundary of'). Choosing the dimension turns this single equation into the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (1 dimension), Green's theorem (2 dimensions), the divergence theorem (flux out of a volume), and the classical curl-form Stokes' theorem — results that look separate in a textbook but are one truth.
depths.deep: The machinery works because the boundary operator ∂ and the exterior derivative d are paired ('adjoint'), and because applying either twice gives nothing: ∂∂ = 0 (the boundary of a boundary is empty) mirrors dd = 0. That duality is the seed of de Rham cohomology, where 'closed forms modulo exact forms' literally counts the holes in a space — so this calculus identity becomes a tool for probing global shape (topology).

atoms.note: The recurring trick is cancellation: every shared interior edge is traversed twice in opposite directions and so cancels, leaving only the outer boundary.
sources: MIT OCW 18.952 Theory of Differential Forms
atoms.art_prompt: a region tiled with small oriented loops whose shared interior edges cancel, leaving one bold loop around the outer boundary

quiz.prompt: In one sentence, what does the generalized Stokes' theorem equate?
quiz.answer: The integral of a differential form ω over the boundary ∂Ω equals the integral of its exterior derivative dω over the region Ω.

quiz.prompt: Which classical theorem does the generalized Stokes' theorem reduce to in one dimension, and how?
quiz.answer: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: with Ω = [a,b] the boundary ∂Ω is the two endpoints {a,b} (with signs), so ∫_Ω df = ∫_{∂Ω} f becomes f(b) − f(a) = ∫_a^b f'.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Here is one identity that secretly contains several famous calculus theorems: whatever a quantity does on the **edge** of a region equals the total of what its **derivative** does throughout the **inside**. Chop the inside into tiny cells; each cell's swirl is shared with its neighbours and cancels, so only the outermost boundary survives. Edge behaviour equals summed interior behaviour.

### Precisely
Using **differential forms** — objects built to be integrated over curves, surfaces, and higher regions — and the **exterior derivative** $d$, the generalized Stokes' theorem says
$$\int_{\partial\Omega}\omega=\int_{\Omega}d\omega,$$
where $\Omega$ is an oriented region and $\partial\Omega$ is its boundary. Specializing the dimension recovers: the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (1D), Green's theorem (2D), the divergence theorem (flux out of a 3D volume), and the classical curl-form Stokes' theorem.

### Worked example
Take the one-dimensional case. Let $\Omega=[a,b]$ and $\omega=f$ a $0$-form (a function), so $d\omega=f'\,dx$. The boundary $\partial[a,b]$ is the two endpoints, oriented as $\{b\}$ minus $\{a\}$. Then
$$\int_{\partial\Omega}\omega=f(b)-f(a),\qquad \int_{\Omega}d\omega=\int_a^b f'\,dx,$$
and Stokes asserts these are equal — which is exactly the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. One template, the familiar result.

### Why it works
The mechanism is **cancellation**. Subdivide $\Omega$ into small oriented cells; on each shared interior face the two neighbouring cells traverse it in *opposite* directions, so those contributions cancel in pairs. Only the unmatched outer faces — the true boundary $\partial\Omega$ — remain. Summing each cell's "interior derivative" therefore collapses to a boundary integral.

### Where it connects
It unifies the `integral`, the `derivative`, and `multivariable-calculus` (grad/curl/div are all $d$ in disguise). It is the capstone of integration on `manifolds`. The pairing $\partial\partial=0$ (boundary of a boundary is empty) mirrors $dd=0$, seeding de Rham cohomology, which counts a space's holes.

### Watch out
Orientation matters: the boundary must be given the induced orientation, and signs flip if you reverse it. The theorem also needs $\Omega$ to be a reasonably nice oriented region with a well-defined boundary — it is not a license to ignore singularities or non-orientable surfaces (like a Möbius band) without care.

atoms.title: Propositional logic and proof
atoms.summary: Logic fixes the rules for combining true/false statements and what counts as a valid deduction; a proof is a finite chain of such deductions from accepted premises.

depths.eli5: Every statement here is simply true or false — no maybes. Logic is the grammar for sticking statements together: 'not', 'and', 'or', and especially 'if this, then that'. A proof is just a careful chain of statements where each link follows from the ones before by a rule everyone agrees on, ending at the thing you wanted to show.
depths.core: Propositional logic builds compound statements from simpler ones using connectives — not (¬), and (∧), or (∨), implies (⇒), and 'if and only if' (⇔) — and works out each compound's truth value from its parts (a 'truth table' lists every case). An argument is valid when its conclusion is true in every situation that makes all the premises true. Two workhorse moves: modus ponens (from 'P' and 'P implies Q', conclude 'Q') and the contrapositive ('P implies Q' is equivalent to 'not-Q implies not-P'), which is the basis of proof by contradiction (assume the opposite and derive nonsense).
depths.deep: There are two different ideas of 'correct': validity (true under every interpretation, a meaning-based notion) and provability (derivable by the formal rules, a syntax-based notion). Gödel's completeness theorem says that for first-order logic these two coincide — every genuinely valid sentence has a finite proof. That exact match (soundness + completeness) is what makes formal reasoning trustworthy; the fact that it does NOT extend to capturing all truths about arithmetic is the seed of Gödel's later incompleteness theorems.

atoms.note: 'P implies Q' is false only in the single case where P is true and Q is false. So a false premise makes the whole implication automatically (vacuously) true.

quiz.prompt: State the contrapositive of P ⇒ Q and explain why it is logically equivalent.
quiz.answer: The contrapositive is ¬Q ⇒ ¬P. Both are false in exactly the same single case (P true, Q false), so they have identical truth tables and are equivalent.

quiz.prompt: An implication P ⇒ Q has a false premise P. Is the implication true or false, and what is this called?
quiz.answer: True — it is vacuously true. An implication is only false when the premise is true and the conclusion false, so a false premise can never falsify it.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Mathematics insists every statement be definitely **true or false** — no maybes. **Logic** is the grammar for combining such statements ("not," "and," "or," and especially "if…then…"), and a **proof** is a careful chain in which each link follows from earlier ones by a rule everyone accepts, ending at the claim you wanted. Logic is what makes mathematical certainty transferable rather than a matter of opinion.

### Precisely
Propositional logic builds compound statements with **connectives**: negation $\lnot$, conjunction $\wedge$ (and), disjunction $\vee$ (or), implication $\Rightarrow$, and biconditional $\Leftrightarrow$. A **truth table** computes a compound's truth value from its parts. An argument is **valid** when its conclusion is true in every row where all premises are true. Two workhorses: **modus ponens** (from $P$ and $P\Rightarrow Q$, infer $Q$) and the **contrapositive**, the equivalence
$$(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv(\lnot Q\Rightarrow \lnot P).$$

### Worked example
Show $P\Rightarrow Q$ and $\lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ are equivalent via truth tables. The implication $P\Rightarrow Q$ is false **only** in the single case $P$ true, $Q$ false. Now check $\lnot Q\Rightarrow\lnot P$ in that same case: $\lnot Q$ is true, $\lnot P$ is false, so the implication is false — and in every *other* case it is true. The two columns match in all four rows, so the statements are logically identical. This equivalence is the engine of **proof by contrapositive**.

### Why it works
There are two notions of "correct": **validity** (true under every interpretation — a meaning-based idea) and **provability** (derivable by the formal rules — a syntax-based idea). Gödel's *completeness* theorem says that for first-order logic these coincide: every valid sentence has a finite proof. That match (soundness plus completeness) is what makes formal reasoning trustworthy.

### Where it connects
Adding "for all" and "there exists" gives `quantifiers-induction` and first-order logic. The contrapositive and proof by contradiction recur everywhere — e.g. Cantor's diagonal in `set-theory-axioms`, the `computability` halting argument, and `godel-incompleteness`. The failure of completeness to capture *all* arithmetic truths seeds Gödel's incompleteness theorems.

### Watch out
"$P$ implies $Q$" is false **only** when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false. So a *false premise* makes the implication automatically (vacuously) true — "if $2+2=5$ then I am the king" is a true statement. This trips up beginners constantly: an implication is not a claim that $P$ holds, only a promise about what follows *if* it does.

atoms.title: Quantifiers and induction
atoms.summary: Quantifiers (for all, there exists) let statements range over infinite domains; induction proves a 'for all natural numbers' claim by a base case plus a step that passes truth up the ladder.

depths.eli5: Two words let a single sentence talk about infinitely many things: 'for all' (every single one) and 'there exists' (at least one). Induction is the domino trick for proving something holds for every counting number: knock over the first domino (show it works for the starting number), then show each domino knocks over the next (if it works for one number, it works for the next) — and every domino falls.
depths.core: Predicate logic adds two quantifiers ranging over a collection (the 'domain'): ∀ ('for all', universal) and ∃ ('there exists', existential). Their order matters — '∀x ∃y' (for each x, some y) is not the same as '∃y ∀x' (one y for all x). Mathematical induction proves a 'for all natural numbers' statement P(n) in two steps: the base case (check P at the starting value, say P(0)) and the inductive step (prove that whenever P(n) holds, P(n+1) holds too). 'Strong' induction lets you assume P is true for all smaller values at once; it is equivalent but often more convenient.
depths.deep: Induction is logically equivalent to the well-ordering principle (every non-empty set of natural numbers has a smallest member), and it is built into the very definition of the natural numbers as one of the Peano axioms — it is not something you can derive without assuming it. It is the finite human's lever on genuine infinity: a two-line argument certifies infinitely many cases at once.

atoms.note: The inductive step proves an implication, not P(n) by itself: you get to ASSUME P(n) for free (the 'inductive hypothesis') and only have to deliver P(n+1).

quiz.prompt: What are the two parts of a proof by mathematical induction?
quiz.answer: A base case establishing P at the starting value, and an inductive step proving P(n) ⇒ P(n+1) for all n; together they yield P(n) for all n.

quiz.prompt: Why does swapping the quantifier order in 'for all x there exists y with y > x' change the meaning?
quiz.answer: ∀x∃y (y>x) is true over the reals (pick y depending on x), but ∃y∀x (y>x) claims one fixed y beats every x, which is false — order decides whether y may depend on x.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Two small words let a single sentence speak about infinitely many objects: **"for all"** (every one) and **"there exists"** (at least one). And **induction** is the domino trick: to prove a statement for *every* counting number, knock over the first domino and show each domino topples the next — then all of them fall, no matter how many there are.

### Precisely
Predicate logic adds quantifiers ranging over a **domain**: the universal $\forall$ and existential $\exists$. Their **order matters**: $\forall x\,\exists y\,R(x,y)$ (each $x$ gets its own $y$) differs from $\exists y\,\forall x\,R(x,y)$ (one $y$ works for all $x$). **Mathematical induction** proves $\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\,P(n)$ from two pieces:
$$\big(P(0)\ \wedge\ \forall n\,(P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1))\big)\ \Rightarrow\ \forall n\,P(n).$$
The first conjunct is the **base case**; the second is the **inductive step**, in which you may *assume* $P(n)$ (the inductive hypothesis) and must derive $P(n+1)$.

### Worked example
Prove $1+2+\cdots+n=\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ for all $n\ge1$. **Base:** $n=1$ gives $1=\tfrac{1\cdot2}{2}=1$. ✓ **Step:** assume $1+\cdots+n=\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Add $n+1$ to both sides:
$$1+\cdots+n+(n+1)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+(n+1)=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2},$$
which is exactly the formula with $n$ replaced by $n+1$. The step holds, so by induction the formula holds for every $n$.

### Why it works
The base starts the chain; the step guarantees each truth passes to its successor. Logically, induction is equivalent to the **well-ordering principle** (every non-empty set of naturals has a least element) and is built into the **Peano axioms** that *define* $\mathbb{N}$ — it cannot be derived without assuming something equivalent to it.

### Where it connects
Induction proves countless results in `combinatorics`, `graph-theory`, and `recurrence-generating`. Quantifier order is the entire content of the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ `limit` (for all $\varepsilon$, there exists $\delta$). Strong induction (assume *all* smaller cases) is equivalent and often handier.

### Watch out
The inductive step proves an **implication**, not $P(n)$ outright — you get $P(n)$ for free and must deliver only $P(n+1)$. And never forget the base case: without it the step proves nothing, the way an endless row of dominoes never falls if no one pushes the first.

atoms.title: Sets, relations, and cardinality
atoms.summary: Modern mathematics is built on sets governed by axioms; relations and equivalence classes organize them, and bijections compare their sizes even when infinite.

depths.eli5: Almost everything in math can be packaged as a 'set' — a collection of objects. To compare the sizes of two collections, try to pair them up one item to one item with nothing left over. If you can, they are the same size — and astonishingly this still works when both collections are endless.
depths.core: Modern math rests on a list of rules called the Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms, usually taken 'with choice' and abbreviated ZFC. They spell out exactly which sets exist and how to build new ones, carefully avoiding paradoxes (like Russell's paradox: 'the set of all sets that don't contain themselves' leads to contradiction). A relation is just a set of pairs (a subset of all pairs A×B), capturing which things relate to which. An equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) chops a set into disjoint groups called classes. Cardinality compares sizes by bijection (perfect one-to-one pairing): two sets are 'equinumerous' (same size) exactly when such a pairing exists.
depths.deep: Cantor's diagonal argument proves the real numbers cannot be listed off against the counting numbers, so the reals form a strictly bigger infinity than the whole numbers — there is an endless hierarchy of larger and larger infinities. The continuum hypothesis (the claim that no size sits strictly between the whole numbers and the reals) was shown to be independent of ZFC by Kurt Gödel and Paul Cohen: the standard axioms genuinely cannot decide it either way.

atoms.note: A 'proper class' (like 'the collection of ALL sets') is too big to itself be a set — and that very restriction is what defuses Russell's paradox.
sources: MIT OCW 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science

resources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Set Theory
