quiz.prompt: When do two sets have the same cardinality, and how does this work for infinite sets?
quiz.answer: When a bijection exists between them; this criterion works for infinite sets too — e.g., the naturals and even numbers are equinumerous despite one containing the other.

quiz.prompt: Sketch why Cantor's diagonal argument shows the reals are uncountable.
quiz.answer: Assume the reals in (0,1) are listed. Build a new number differing from the n-th listed number in its n-th decimal digit; it differs from every listed number, so it was missing — no list can be complete.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Nearly every mathematical object can be packaged as a **set** — a collection of things. To compare two collections' sizes, try to pair them off, one item to one item, nothing left over. If you can, they are the same size. Astonishingly, this pairing test still works for *endless* collections, and it reveals that some infinities are strictly bigger than others.

### Precisely
Modern mathematics rests on the **Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms with choice (ZFC)**, which specify exactly which sets exist and how to build new ones while dodging paradoxes. A **relation** on $A,B$ is a subset of pairs $A\times B$. An **equivalence relation** (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) partitions a set into disjoint **classes**. Two sets have the same **cardinality** when a bijection links them:
$$|A|=|B|\iff \exists\ \text{bijection}\ f\colon A\to B.$$

### Worked example
Show the naturals $\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ and the even naturals $E=\{0,2,4,\dots\}$ have the *same* size, despite $E$ being "half" of $\mathbb{N}$. The map $f(n)=2n$ pairs each natural with an even number: $0\mapsto0,1\mapsto2,2\mapsto4,\dots$ It is injective (different $n$ give different $2n$) and surjective (every even number is some $2n$), hence a bijection. So $|\mathbb{N}|=|E|$ — for infinite sets, a part can match the whole.

### Why it works
Russell's paradox — "the set of all sets that do not contain themselves" — shows naive set-building is inconsistent. ZFC blocks it by forbidding a set of *all* sets; collections too big to be sets are **proper classes**. Within ZFC, **Cantor's diagonal argument** proves the reals cannot be listed against $\mathbb{N}$, so $|\mathbb{R}|>|\mathbb{N}|$ — there is a hierarchy of ever-larger infinities.

### Where it connects
Bijections come straight from `set-function`. Equivalence classes power `modular-arithmetic` and quotients in `homomorphism`. Number systems (`number-systems`) are constructed set-theoretically, and the diagonal trick recurs in `computability` and `godel-incompleteness`.

### Watch out
The **continuum hypothesis** — that no size lies strictly between $|\mathbb{N}|$ and $|\mathbb{R}|$ — was shown by Gödel and Cohen to be **independent** of ZFC: the standard axioms can neither prove nor refute it. And beware: "same cardinality" for infinite sets violates the everyday intuition that a proper subset must be smaller.

atoms.title: Number systems: ℕ to ℂ
atoms.summary: Each number system is built to solve equations the previous one cannot: subtraction births the integers, division the rationals, limits the reals, and square roots of negatives the complex numbers.

depths.eli5: Start with the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 (called the naturals, written ℕ). Want to subtract any time you like and allow negatives? You get the integers ℤ. Want to divide freely and allow fractions? You get the rationals ℚ. Want to fill in every gap on the number line, including endless decimals like π? You get the reals ℝ. Want a square root of −1? Add a new number called i and you get the complex numbers ℂ. Each new layer exists to make one previously-impossible operation possible.
depths.core: ℕ (naturals) lets you add and multiply. ℤ (integers) adds negatives so subtraction always works. ℚ (rationals = fractions) adds reciprocals so division by nonzero numbers works, making ℚ a 'field' (a system where +, −, ×, ÷ all behave). But ℚ has holes — for instance √2 is not any fraction — so ℝ (reals) is its 'completion', filling every gap; technically it adds the limits of Cauchy sequences and gives the least-upper-bound property (every bounded set has a tightest ceiling). ℝ still cannot solve x² = −1, so ℂ (complex numbers) introduces i with i² = −1; once you have ℂ, every polynomial factors completely into linear pieces.
depths.deep: The reals are the one and only 'complete ordered field' — completeness (no missing points) is exactly the property that makes limits, and therefore calculus, work. The complex numbers give up being orderable (you cannot line them up smaller-to-larger in a way that respects arithmetic) in exchange for 'algebraic closure': every degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots there, which is the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

atoms.note: ℝ is uncountable while ℚ is countable, so 'almost every' real number is irrational — the fractions are a vanishingly thin (measure-zero) dusting on the number line.
atoms.art_prompt: nested rings labeled N, Z, Q, R, C, each ring adding a missing operation noted on its edge

quiz.prompt: What operation or property forces each extension: ℤ from ℕ, ℚ from ℤ, ℝ from ℚ, and ℂ from ℝ?
quiz.answer: ℤ closes subtraction (negatives), ℚ closes division (inverses), ℝ closes limits/fills gaps (completeness), and ℂ closes square roots of negatives (algebraic closure).

quiz.prompt: What does the reals possess that the rationals lack, and why does calculus need it?
quiz.answer: Completeness — the least-upper-bound property, so every bounded sequence has the limits it should. Without it, expected limits (and √2) would be 'missing,' and limits/derivatives could fail to exist.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Each number system exists to make one previously-impossible operation possible. Start with the counting numbers. Want to subtract freely? Add negatives. Want to divide freely? Add fractions. Want to fill every gap on the line, including $\pi$ and $\sqrt2$? Add the irrationals. Want a square root of $-1$? Invent $i$. Mathematics grows by closing operations that the current numbers refuse to perform.

### Precisely
The chain is
$$\mathbb{N}\subset\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{R}\subset\mathbb{C}.$$
$\mathbb{N}$ (naturals) supports $+,\times$. $\mathbb{Z}$ (integers) adds negatives so subtraction always works. $\mathbb{Q}$ (rationals, i.e. fractions) adds reciprocals, making it a **field** ($+,-,\times,\div$ all behave). $\mathbb{R}$ (reals) is the **completion** of $\mathbb{Q}$ — it fills every gap and gives the **least-upper-bound property**. $\mathbb{C}$ (complex) adjoins $i$ with $i^2=-1$, making the system **algebraically closed**.

### Worked example
Show $\mathbb{Q}$ has a hole: $\sqrt2$ is not a fraction. Suppose $\sqrt2=p/q$ in lowest terms. Then $p^2=2q^2$, so $p^2$ is even, so $p$ is even, say $p=2k$. Then $4k^2=2q^2$, i.e. $q^2=2k^2$, so $q$ is even too — contradicting "lowest terms." Hence no fraction squares to $2$; the rationals are missing this point, and $\mathbb{R}$ is built precisely to include it (as the limit of $1,1.4,1.41,1.414,\dots$).

### Why it works
$\mathbb{R}$ is the **unique complete ordered field**: completeness (no missing points) is exactly the property that makes limits — and therefore all of calculus — work. $\mathbb{C}$ surrenders orderability (you cannot line complex numbers up smaller-to-larger consistently) in exchange for algebraic closure: every degree-$n$ polynomial has $n$ roots there.

### Where it connects
Completeness underlies the `limit`, `real-analysis`, and `metric-space`. Algebraic closure of $\mathbb{C}$ is the `fundamental-theorem-algebra`. The construction relies on `set-theory-axioms`; the arithmetic-of-remainders branch is `modular-arithmetic`; $\mathbb{C}$ unfolds in `complex-numbers`.

### Watch out
$\mathbb{R}$ is **uncountable** while $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, so "almost every" real is irrational — the fractions are a vanishingly thin (measure-zero) dusting on the line. Don't picture the rationals as filling most of the number line; they are full of holes, and the reals are overwhelmingly the irrationals.

atoms.title: Modular arithmetic
atoms.summary: Modular arithmetic works with remainders after division by a fixed modulus, turning the integers into finite cyclic systems where clock-like wraparound is the rule.

depths.eli5: Think of a clock. Five hours after 9 o'clock is not 14 o'clock — it wraps around to 2 o'clock. Modular arithmetic is arithmetic that wraps around like this after hitting a fixed number called the modulus (12 for a clock). You keep only the remainder after dividing. So '14 on a 12-clock' becomes 2.
depths.core: Two whole numbers are 'congruent mod n' (written a ≡ b mod n) when they leave the same remainder after dividing by n — equivalently, when n divides their difference. This is an equivalence relation, and grouping numbers by their remainder produces a finite system written ℤ/nℤ (the integers mod n), which is a 'ring' (you can add, subtract, multiply). Because addition and multiplication respect congruence, you may reduce mod n at any point in a calculation. When n is a prime number, ℤ/nℤ is even a field — every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse (you can divide) — which is the basis of Fermat's little theorem.
depths.deep: The Chinese remainder theorem says that for n = m·k with m and k sharing no common factor (coprime), the system ℤ/mkℤ splits into the independent pair ℤ/mℤ × ℤ/kℤ, which lets computations run in parallel. These finite systems are the backbone of public-key cryptography: the RSA algorithm's security relies on the fact that raising to a power mod n is fast, while undoing it (which would require factoring n) is believed to be extremely slow.

atoms.note: Division is delicate mod n: you can divide by a number a only when a shares no common factor with n (they are 'coprime'). That is exactly why prime moduli — where every nonzero number qualifies — are so convenient.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Think of a clock. Five hours after $9$ o'clock is not $14$ o'clock — it wraps around to $2$. **Modular arithmetic** is arithmetic that wraps around after a fixed number, the **modulus**. You keep only the **remainder** after dividing. This turns the infinite integers into small, finite, cyclic worlds — and those finite worlds are the backbone of modern cryptography.

### Precisely
For a positive integer $n$, two integers are **congruent mod $n$**,
$$a\equiv b\pmod n\iff n\mid(a-b),$$
i.e. they leave the same remainder on division by $n$. This is an equivalence relation; grouping integers by remainder gives the finite **ring** $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ with $n$ elements, where you may add, subtract, and multiply, reducing mod $n$ at any step. When $n$ is **prime**, $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is a **field**: every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.

### Worked example
Compute $7\times 8 \bmod 5$. Reduce first: $7\equiv2$ and $8\equiv3\pmod5$. Then $7\times8\equiv2\times3=6\equiv1\pmod5$. So $7\times8$ leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $5$ — and indeed $56=11\cdot5+1$. Reducing before multiplying gave the same answer with far smaller numbers, which is exactly why modular arithmetic scales to cryptographic sizes.

### Why it works
Congruence is preserved by $+$ and $\times$: if $a\equiv a'$ and $b\equiv b'$, then $a+b\equiv a'+b'$ and $ab\equiv a'b'$. That is what licenses reducing mod $n$ at any point. Division is the subtle part: you can divide by $a$ only when $a$ is **coprime** to $n$ (shares no factor), because only then does $a$ have an inverse. Prime moduli make *every* nonzero element qualify.

### Where it connects
It is the prototype of quotient structures in `homomorphism` and `ring-field` ($\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ quotiented by multiples of $n$). The Chinese remainder theorem splits $\mathbb{Z}/mk\mathbb{Z}$ into independent pieces. RSA cryptography exploits that exponentiating mod $n$ is fast while reversing it (factoring $n$) is believed hard.

### Watch out
Division mod $n$ can simply fail. In $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$, the number $2$ has no inverse, and worse, $2\times3\equiv0$ even though neither factor is $0$ — these "zero divisors" exist precisely because $6$ is not prime. Always check coprimality before "dividing" modularly.

atoms.title: Polynomials and roots
atoms.summary: A polynomial is a finite sum of scaled powers; its roots are where it vanishes, and each root corresponds to a linear factor, linking algebra to geometry.

depths.eli5: A polynomial is an expression like 3x² − 5x + 2 — powers of x, each scaled by a number, added up. Graphed, it makes a smooth curve. Its 'roots' are the x-values where the curve touches zero (crosses the horizontal axis). Each root r lets you peel off a simple factor (x − r), the way 6 factors into 2 × 3.
depths.core: A polynomial is a finite sum aₙxⁿ + … + a₁x + a₀; the highest power n is its degree. The factor theorem says r is a root (i.e. p(r) = 0) exactly when (x − r) divides p evenly — so a degree-n polynomial has at most n roots. Polynomial long division plus the remainder theorem (dividing p by x − r leaves remainder p(r)) make finding and removing roots systematic. Over a field, polynomials form a ring with unique factorization into 'irreducibles' (pieces that cannot be factored further), exactly mirroring how integers factor uniquely into primes.
depths.deep: Whether the roots can be written using only +, −, ×, ÷ and nth roots ('by radicals') depends on the symmetry group of the roots. Galois theory shows the general degree-5 polynomial (the quintic) has no radical formula because that symmetry group is not 'solvable' — a landmark negative result. Existence of the roots themselves is only guaranteed once you allow complex numbers, by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

atoms.note: Counting roots 'with multiplicity' is what makes 'a degree-n polynomial has n roots' exactly true — a double root (a point the curve just touches) counts twice.

quiz.answer: Its roots are 2 and 3 (they sum to 5 and multiply to 6), so x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A **polynomial** is built from powers of $x$, each scaled and added: things like $3x^2-5x+2$. Graphed, it traces a smooth curve. Its **roots** are where the curve hits zero (crosses the horizontal axis). The key idea is that each root lets you peel off a simple factor — the way the number $6$ splits into $2\times3$, a polynomial splits into linear pieces.

### Precisely
A polynomial is $p(x)=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$ with $a_n\ne0$; the top power $n$ is its **degree**. The **factor theorem** states
$$p(r)=0\iff (x-r)\mid p(x),$$
so $r$ is a root exactly when $(x-r)$ divides $p$ evenly. The **remainder theorem** adds that dividing $p$ by $x-r$ leaves remainder $p(r)$. Consequently a degree-$n$ polynomial has **at most $n$ roots**, and over a field, polynomials factor uniquely into **irreducibles** — mirroring prime factorization of integers.

### Worked example
Factor $x^2-5x+6$ by finding its roots. We seek two numbers that **sum to $5$** (the coefficient of $x$, negated) and **multiply to $6$** (the constant): those are $2$ and $3$. Check: $2+3=5$, $2\times3=6$. So the roots are $x=2$ and $x=3$, and by the factor theorem
$$x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3).$$
Expanding confirms it. The two linear factors are precisely the "peeled-off" pieces, one per root.

### Why it works
Polynomial long division shows $p(x)=(x-r)q(x)+R$ for a constant remainder $R$; setting $x=r$ gives $R=p(r)$. So $p(r)=0$ forces $R=0$, meaning $(x-r)$ divides $p$ cleanly — that is the factor theorem. Repeating peels off one factor per root.

### Where it connects
Existence of roots is guaranteed only over $\mathbb{C}$ (`fundamental-theorem-algebra`). Whether roots are expressible "by radicals" depends on the symmetry group of the roots (Galois theory): the general quintic has no radical formula. Polynomial rings exemplify `ring-field` and unique factorization, paralleling `modular-arithmetic`.

### Watch out
Count roots **with multiplicity** to make "$n$ roots for degree $n$" exactly true: a double root, where the curve just touches the axis (like $x^2=(x-0)^2$), counts twice. And over $\mathbb{R}$ a polynomial may have *fewer* real roots than its degree (e.g. $x^2+1$ has none) — you need $\mathbb{C}$ for the full count.

atoms.title: Counting and combinatorics
atoms.summary: Combinatorics is the art of counting arrangements and selections without listing them, built from the multiplication principle, permutations, and combinations.

depths.eli5: How many ways can you arrange or pick a bunch of things? Combinatorics is the art of counting these without listing them all out. If the order matters (like a race podium: gold-silver-bronze) you count 'permutations'; if it does not (like picking a team) you count 'combinations'. There are tidy formulas for both.
depths.core: The multiplication principle says: if one choice has a ways and an independent next choice has b ways, together they have a×b ways. From it: permutations P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)! count ordered selections of k items from n (here n! means 'n factorial', n × (n−1) × … × 1); combinations C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) count unordered selections and are called the binomial coefficients ('n choose k'). The binomial theorem, (a+b)ⁿ = Σ C(n,k) aᵏ bⁿ⁻ᵏ, links these counts to algebra. Inclusion–exclusion is a correction rule that avoids double-counting when groups overlap.
depths.deep: Many counting identities have two proofs: an algebraic one (push symbols around) and a bijective one (exhibit a one-to-one correspondence between two sets, proving them equal in size) — the bijective proof is usually the more illuminating. Generating functions encode an entire sequence of counts as the coefficients of a single power series, converting recurrences into ordinary algebra — the doorway to analytic combinatorics.

atoms.note: C(n,k) = C(n,n−k): choosing which k items to include is the same as choosing which n−k to leave out — so the two counts must match.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
How many ways can you arrange or select a collection of things — without tediously listing them all? **Combinatorics** answers such questions with formulas. If **order matters** (a race podium: gold, silver, bronze), you count **permutations**. If order does *not* matter (choosing a committee), you count **combinations**. A few principles generate the whole subject.

### Precisely
The **multiplication principle**: if one choice has $a$ options and an independent next choice has $b$, together they have $a\times b$. From it: **permutations** $P(n,k)=\dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}$ count ordered selections of $k$ from $n$ (where $n!=n(n-1)\cdots1$); **combinations** $\binom{n}{k}=\dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$ count unordered selections. The **binomial theorem** $(a+b)^n=\sum_k\binom{n}{k}a^kb^{n-k}$ links these counts to algebra.

### Worked example
How many $3$-person committees from $6$ people? Order does not matter, so use combinations:
$$\binom{6}{3}=\frac{6!}{3!\,3!}=\frac{720}{6\cdot6}=20.$$
Contrast with *ranking* $3$ of the $6$ (chair, vice-chair, secretary — order matters): $P(6,3)=\frac{6!}{3!}=120$. The committee count is smaller by a factor of $3!=6$, exactly the number of orderings of $3$ people that all give the *same* committee.

### Why it works
The relationship $P(n,k)=k!\,\binom{n}{k}$ explains the division by $k!$: every unordered selection corresponds to $k!$ ordered ones, so dividing the ordered count by $k!$ recovers the unordered one. This is a **bijective** argument — pairing objects to prove counts equal — usually more illuminating than pushing symbols.

### Where it connects
Binomial coefficients feed `probability` (counting equally likely outcomes) and `random-variables`. The symmetry $\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n}{n-k}$ (choosing whom to include = choosing whom to exclude) appears all over. Generating functions in `recurrence-generating` encode entire count-sequences as power series.

### Watch out
Decide carefully whether order matters and whether repetition is allowed — these choose between four different formulas. A classic error is using $\binom{n}{k}$ when arrangements are actually distinct, or vice versa. And inclusion–exclusion is needed whenever the things you count **overlap**, to avoid double-counting.

atoms.title: Probability axioms
atoms.summary: Probability assigns numbers in [0,1] to events under three axioms; from them flow conditional probability, independence, and Bayes' rule for updating belief.

depths.eli5: Probability is a number measuring how likely something is, on a scale from 0 (it never happens) to 1 (it always happens). The basic rules are common sense: something is guaranteed to happen (total probability 1), a chance can never be negative, and if two things can't happen together, the chance of one-or-the-other is just their chances added up.
depths.core: An 'event' is a set of possible outcomes drawn from the 'sample space' (all possible outcomes). Kolmogorov's three axioms — probabilities are non-negative, the whole sample space has probability 1, and the probability of several mutually exclusive ('disjoint') events combined is the sum of their probabilities — make probability a 'measure'. Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) is the chance of A once you know B happened (∩ means 'and'). Two events are 'independent' when P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B), i.e. knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Bayes' rule, P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B), flips a conditional around and is the formal recipe for updating your beliefs after seeing evidence.
depths.deep: Random variables move probability onto the number line, and their average ('expectation') is a Lebesgue integral against the probability distribution — which is exactly why measure theory is the rigorous foundation of probability. Two capstone theorems explain the everyday world: the law of large numbers (averages settle down as you collect more data) and the central limit theorem (those averages tend to follow the bell-shaped Gaussian curve, no matter the original shape).

atoms.note: Independence and disjointness are opposite extremes, not the same thing: two disjoint events with nonzero probability are maximally dependent, because one happening makes the other impossible.

quiz.answer: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B); it inverts a conditional probability, letting you update the probability of a cause A given observed evidence B.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Probability puts a number on **how likely** something is, from $0$ (never) to $1$ (always). The basic rules are common sense made precise: something is certain to happen, a chance is never negative, and if two outcomes cannot co-occur, the chance of one-or-the-other is just the sum of their chances. From these flow the tools for reasoning under uncertainty and updating beliefs on evidence.

### Precisely
An **event** is a subset of the **sample space** $\Omega$ of all outcomes. **Kolmogorov's axioms**: $P(A)\ge0$; $P(\Omega)=1$; and for **disjoint** events, $P\big(\bigcup_i A_i\big)=\sum_i P(A_i)$. **Conditional probability** is $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$. Events are **independent** when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. **Bayes' rule**,
$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)},$$
inverts a conditional and is the recipe for updating belief.

### Worked example
A test for a disease is $99\%$ accurate, and $1\%$ of people have the disease. You test positive — what is the chance you are actually sick? Let $A$ = sick, $B$ = positive. $P(A)=0.01$, $P(B\mid A)=0.99$, and $P(B\mid \text{not }A)=0.01$. Total positive rate $P(B)=0.99\cdot0.01+0.01\cdot0.99=0.0198$. Bayes:
$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{0.99\cdot0.01}{0.0198}=0.5.$$
Only $50\%$ — because the disease is rare, false positives roughly match true positives. This counterintuitive result is the "base rate" lesson.

### Why it works
The axioms make probability a **measure** (a way to assign consistent sizes), so all of measure theory's machinery applies. Bayes' rule is just algebra on the definition of conditioning: $P(A\cap B)$ can be written two ways, $P(A\mid B)P(B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)$, and solving for $P(A\mid B)$ gives the formula.

### Where it connects
Counting equally likely outcomes uses `combinatorics`. Putting probability on the number line gives `random-variables`. The rigorous foundation is `measure-theory` (a probability is a measure of total mass $1$). Aggregate behaviour is governed by the law of large numbers and the `central-limit-theorem`.

### Watch out
**Independence is not disjointness** — they are opposite extremes. Two disjoint events with nonzero probability are maximally *dependent*: if one happens the other cannot, so $P(A\mid B)=0\ne P(A)$. Confusing the two is among the most common probability errors.

atoms.title: Random variables and expectation
atoms.summary: A random variable turns outcomes into numbers; expectation is its probability-weighted average, and variance measures its spread, with linearity of expectation as the workhorse.

depths.eli5: A random variable is just a number whose value is decided by chance — like the result of a die roll, which could be 1 through 6. Its 'expectation' is the average you'd get if you repeated the experiment forever (3.5 for a fair die). Its 'variance' tells you how wildly the result tends to swing around that average — small variance means it stays near the average, big variance means it jumps around a lot.
depths.core: A random variable X assigns a number to each chance outcome, and its 'distribution' lists how likely each value is (a pmf — probability mass function — for discrete cases like dice, a pdf — probability density function — for continuous ones). The expectation E[X] is the probability-weighted average. A crucial fact is linearity: E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always, even if X and Y influence each other — which turns many hard counting problems into easy sums. Variance, Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²] = E[X²] − E[X]², measures spread; its square root, the standard deviation, brings the spread back into the original units.
depths.deep: The law of large numbers says that as you collect more samples, their average homes in on E[X]. The central limit theorem says the leftover wobble, once rescaled by √n (the square root of the sample count), looks Gaussian (bell-shaped) regardless of the original distribution — which is why the normal curve shows up everywhere. Together these two theorems are the bridge from unpredictable individual randomness to highly predictable aggregate behavior.

atoms.note: Linearity of expectation requires NO independence — that is exactly why it is so powerful for combinatorial counting, where the pieces often interact.

quiz.prompt: Why is linearity of expectation so useful, and what condition does it require?
quiz.answer: E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] always holds, with no independence required, so you can split a complicated random quantity into simple pieces and add their averages.

quiz.prompt: A fair die is rolled. What is the expected value of the result?

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A **random variable** is just a number whose value is decided by chance — the result of a die roll, tomorrow's temperature, a measurement error. Its **expectation** is the long-run average you would get by repeating the experiment forever. Its **variance** measures how wildly the value swings around that average. Together, mean and spread summarize most of what you need to know about a random quantity.

### Precisely
A random variable $X$ assigns a number to each outcome; its **distribution** gives the probabilities of its values (a pmf $P(X=x)$ in the discrete case, a density $f(x)$ in the continuous case). The **expectation** is
$$E[X]=\sum_x x\,P(X=x)\quad\text{or}\quad E[X]=\int x\,f(x)\,dx.$$
**Linearity** holds always: $E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]$, even when $X,Y$ are dependent. The **variance** is $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-E[X])^2]=E[X^2]-E[X]^2$, and its square root is the standard deviation.

### Worked example
Roll a fair die. $X$ takes values $1,\dots,6$ each with probability $\tfrac16$. Then
$$E[X]=\frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6}=\frac{21}{6}=3.5.$$
For the variance, $E[X^2]=\tfrac16(1+4+9+16+25+36)=\tfrac{91}{6}$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\tfrac{91}{6}-3.5^2=\tfrac{91}{6}-12.25\approx2.92$, giving a standard deviation $\approx1.71$. The expected value $3.5$ is not an attainable roll — it is the average over many rolls.

### Why it works
Linearity of expectation follows directly from the definition as a sum/integral, which respects addition regardless of any relationship between $X$ and $Y$. This is what makes it astonishingly powerful for `combinatorics`: split a complicated random count into simple indicator pieces and add their (easy) averages.

### Where it connects
Continuous expectations are `integral`s (and rigorously, `measure-theory` integrals). The law of large numbers says sample averages converge to $E[X]$; the `central-limit-theorem` says their fluctuations are Gaussian. Variance and covariance underpin `orthogonality-least-squares` and PCA via `svd`.

### Watch out
Linearity needs **no independence** — that is precisely its strength — but the corresponding rule for *variance*, $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)$, *does* require independence (or zero covariance). Don't apply the variance sum rule to dependent variables.

atoms.title: Rings and fields
atoms.summary: A ring has two compatible operations — addition (a group) and multiplication (associative, distributing over addition); a field is a ring where every nonzero element is invertible.

depths.eli5: A 'ring' is a number system where you can add, subtract, and multiply — the integers (…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …) are the model example. A 'field' is a ring where you can also divide by anything except zero — like the fractions or the real numbers. The catch is that addition and multiplication must cooperate through the distributive rule, a·(b+c) = a·b + a·c.
depths.core: A ring is a set that is an abelian group under addition (so + is commutative and every element has a negative) together with a multiplication that is associative and distributes over addition. The familiar 'commutative rings with identity' (multiplication commutes and there is a number 1), such as the integers ℤ and rings of polynomials, are where most ordinary arithmetic lives. A field adds one more demand: multiplication, restricted to the nonzero elements, is also a group — meaning every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse, so you can divide. The rationals ℚ, reals ℝ, complex numbers ℂ, and the integers-mod-a-prime ℤ/pℤ are all fields.
depths.deep: An 'ideal' is to a ring what a normal subgroup is to a group: the special kind of subset you are allowed to 'quotient out' by. The quotient ring R/I generalizes modular arithmetic (the integers mod n are exactly ℤ quotiented by the ideal of multiples of n), and an ideal is 'maximal' precisely when the quotient comes out a field. This toolkit — ideals, quotients, and structure-preserving maps (homomorphisms) — is the shared language behind number theory, algebraic geometry, and error-correcting codes.

atoms.note: Every field is a ring, but the integers ℤ are a ring that is NOT a field — they lack a dividing inverse for everything except ±1 (you can't get 1/2 inside ℤ).

quiz.prompt: What single property separates a field from a general commutative ring with identity?
quiz.answer: In a field every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse (you can divide); a general ring need not have this — e.g., ℤ.

quiz.prompt: Is ℤ/6ℤ a field? Why or why not?
quiz.answer: No — 6 is not prime, so 2 and 3 are nonzero yet 2×3 ≡ 0; zero divisors exist and 2 has no inverse, so it fails to be a field.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A **ring** is a number system where you can add, subtract, and multiply — the integers are the model. A **field** is a ring where you can *also* divide by anything except zero — like the fractions or the reals. The crucial requirement is that the two operations cooperate through the **distributive law**, $a(b+c)=ab+ac$, which is what links addition and multiplication into a single coherent arithmetic.

### Precisely
A **ring** $R$ is an abelian group under $+$ (so addition is commutative and every element has a negative) together with a multiplication that is associative and **distributes** over addition. A *commutative ring with identity* additionally has $ab=ba$ and an element $1$. A **field** demands one thing more: every **nonzero** element has a multiplicative inverse,
$$a\ne0\Rightarrow\exists\,a^{-1}\ \text{with}\ aa^{-1}=1,$$
so you can divide. Examples: $\mathbb{Z}$ is a ring (not a field); $\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}$, and $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ (prime $p$) are fields.

### Worked example
Is $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ a field? It is certainly a ring. But $6$ is not prime, and there we find $2\times3\equiv0\pmod6$ with neither factor zero — a **zero divisor**. If $2$ had an inverse $u$, then $3\equiv u\cdot2\cdot3\equiv u\cdot0=0$, false. So $2$ is not invertible and $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ is **not** a field. By contrast $\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}$ *is*: $2\cdot3=6\equiv1$, so $2^{-1}=3$, and every nonzero element similarly has an inverse.

### Why it works
A field is exactly a commutative ring whose nonzero elements form a group under multiplication. Primality of the modulus rules out zero divisors (if $p$ is prime and $p\mid ab$ then $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$), which is precisely what is needed for every nonzero residue to be invertible.

### Where it connects
Fields are the scalars of every `vector-space`. The integers-mod-$n$ come from `modular-arithmetic`. **Ideals** generalize "multiples of $n$," and quotient rings $R/I$ generalize modular arithmetic — the bridge to `homomorphism`. Polynomial rings (`polynomials-roots`) and the `fundamental-theorem-algebra` live here.

### Watch out
Every field is a ring, but **not every ring is a field**: $\mathbb{Z}$ lacks inverses for all but $\pm1$ (no $\tfrac12$ inside). And a ring can have zero divisors — nonzero elements multiplying to zero — which never happens in a field. Spotting zero divisors is the quickest way to disqualify a candidate field.

atoms.title: Homomorphisms and quotients
atoms.summary: A homomorphism is a structure-preserving map between algebraic objects; its kernel measures what it collapses, and the isomorphism theorem says the quotient by the kernel is a faithful copy of the image.

depths.eli5: A homomorphism is a translation between two number systems that keeps the arithmetic intact: whether you combine two things first and then translate, or translate first and then combine, you land in the same place. The set of things it flattens down to the 'do-nothing' element is called its kernel — and the size of that kernel measures exactly how much information the translation throws away.
depths.core: A homomorphism φ is a map between two algebraic structures that respects their operation: φ(a·b) = φ(a)·φ(b). Its kernel — everything that gets sent to the identity element — turns out to be a normal subgroup (for groups) or an ideal (for rings); its image — everything it actually produces — is a substructure of the target. The first isomorphism theorem, G/ker φ ≅ im φ, says: if you quotient out (collapse together) exactly what the map forgets, you recover a perfect copy of what it sees. In other words, collapsing and embedding are two views of the same map. ('≅' means 'is isomorphic to' — structurally identical.)
depths.deep: This is the organizing principle of all of algebra: classify objects only up to isomorphism (treat structurally identical things as the same), and read every map as an embedding glued to a quotient. Pushed further — tracking kernels and cokernels and asking when chains of maps are 'exact' — it grows into homological algebra, which exports this same bookkeeping into topology and geometry.

atoms.note: Normality of the kernel is not a technicality — it is exactly the condition that makes the quotient G/ker φ a group in the first place.

quiz.prompt: What does the first isomorphism theorem state?
quiz.answer: For a homomorphism φ: G→H, the quotient G/ker φ is isomorphic to the image im φ — quotienting by what the map collapses gives a faithful copy of what it produces.

quiz.answer: The map is injective: distinct elements stay distinct, since only the identity maps to the identity, so G embeds as a copy inside the target.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A **homomorphism** is a translation between two algebraic systems that keeps the arithmetic intact: combine first then translate, or translate first then combine — either way you land in the same place. The set of elements it flattens to the "do-nothing" element is its **kernel**, and the size of that kernel measures exactly how much information the translation discards.

### Precisely
A map $\varphi\colon G\to H$ is a **homomorphism** if it respects the operation: $\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$. Its **kernel** $\ker\varphi=\{g:\varphi(g)=e_H\}$ is a normal subgroup (for groups) or an ideal (for rings); its **image** $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ is a substructure of $H$. The **first isomorphism theorem** says
$$G/\ker\varphi\ \cong\ \operatorname{im}\varphi,$$
i.e. quotienting out what the map forgets reproduces a perfect copy of what it sees. ($\cong$ means "isomorphic" — structurally identical.)

### Worked example
Let $\varphi\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ send each integer to its remainder mod $3$. It is a homomorphism: $\varphi(a+b)=(a+b)\bmod3=\varphi(a)+\varphi(b)$. The kernel is the integers sent to $0$ — the multiples of $3$, written $3\mathbb{Z}$. The image is all of $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$. The theorem then reads $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ — collapsing $\mathbb{Z}$ by its multiples-of-$3$ kernel gives exactly the three-element image, confirming the principle on a concrete case.

### Why it works
Elements with the same image differ by something in the kernel, so the image "sees" precisely the cosets of the kernel — and the set of cosets *is* the quotient $G/\ker\varphi$. Matching cosets to images is the isomorphism. Normality of the kernel is exactly the condition that makes $G/\ker\varphi$ a group in the first place.

### Where it connects
This is the organizing principle of all algebra: classify objects up to isomorphism, and read every map as a quotient glued to an embedding. It generalizes `modular-arithmetic` and `ring-field` quotients, builds on `group`, and grows into homological algebra and `category-theory` (where homomorphisms become morphisms).

### Watch out
A homomorphism is **injective iff its kernel is trivial** (just the identity): only then do distinct elements stay distinct. So a large kernel means heavy information loss. And the *image*, not the whole codomain $H$, is what the isomorphism theorem matches — $\varphi$ need not be onto all of $H$.

atoms.title: Complex numbers and Euler's formula
atoms.summary: Complex numbers extend the reals with i (√−1); Euler's formula fuses the exponential with trigonometry, revealing rotation and oscillation as one phenomenon.

depths.eli5: Invent a brand-new number, called i, whose square is −1 (no ordinary number does that). Suddenly every equation has solutions. If you plot these numbers as points on a flat plane, multiplying by i turns out to be a quarter-turn rotation. So complex multiplication literally IS rotation — which is why waves, circles, and anything that spins are naturally described with complex numbers.
depths.core: A complex number a + bi is a point in the plane, with two natural descriptions: a 'modulus' |z| (its distance from the origin, i.e. its length) and an 'argument' arg z (the angle it makes). Multiplying two complex numbers multiplies their lengths and ADDS their angles — that is what makes rotation algebraic. Euler's formula, e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ (provable by lining up the Taylor series of both sides), folds all of trigonometry into the exponential function. Its famous special case e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 ties together five fundamental constants (e, i, π, 1, 0) in one line.
depths.deep: Complex functions that are merely once-differentiable in the complex sense (called holomorphic) turn out to be automatically infinitely differentiable and exactly equal to their own power series — a rigidity with no counterpart for real-variable functions. This surprising strength is why complex analysis delivers the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, lets you evaluate hard real integrals via loop ('contour') integrals, and supports 'analytic continuation', the trick that extends the Riemann zeta function beyond where its defining sum converges.

atoms.note: Powers and roots become easy in 'polar form' (length-and-angle) via de Moivre's theorem: the n-th roots of 1 ('roots of unity') sit as equally spaced points around the unit circle.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Invent a number $i$ whose square is $-1$ — no ordinary number does that — and suddenly every polynomial equation has solutions. Plot these numbers as points in a plane and something magical appears: multiplying by $i$ rotates by a quarter turn. So complex multiplication literally **is** rotation, which is why anything that spins, waves, or oscillates is most naturally described with complex numbers.

### Precisely
A complex number $z=a+bi$ is a point in the plane with **modulus** $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ (distance from origin) and **argument** $\arg z$ (angle). Multiplication multiplies moduli and **adds** arguments. **Euler's formula** unites exponentials and trigonometry:
$$e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta,$$
whose special case is the celebrated $e^{i\pi}+1=0$, tying together $e,i,\pi,1,0$.

### Worked example
Evaluate $e^{i\pi}$ from Euler's formula. Set $\theta=\pi$: $e^{i\pi}=\cos\pi+i\sin\pi=-1+i\cdot0=-1$. Rearranged, $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. Geometrically, $e^{i\pi}$ means "rotate the point $1$ counterclockwise by $\pi$ radians (a half-turn)," landing on $-1$. Multiplying by $e^{i\theta}$ always rotates by $\theta$ without changing length — that is the content of the formula.

### Why it works
Euler's formula is proved by comparing **Taylor series** (`taylor`): expand $e^{i\theta}$, and separate real and imaginary parts; the real part reproduces the cosine series and the imaginary part the sine series. Because multiplication adds arguments, $e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta}=e^{i(\alpha+\beta)}$ encodes the angle-addition laws of trigonometry in one stroke.

### Where it connects
$\mathbb{C}$ completes the `number-systems` chain and is algebraically closed (`fundamental-theorem-algebra`). Euler's formula is the engine of `fourier` analysis (orthogonal exponentials) and `trigonometry`. Complex differentiability is astonishingly rigid (`complex-analysis`): one derivative forces infinite smoothness.

### Watch out
$\mathbb{C}$ cannot be **ordered** compatibly with its arithmetic — there is no consistent "less than," so inequalities like $z<w$ are meaningless for non-real complex numbers. Use the **modulus** $|z|$ when you need a notion of size. Also, the argument is only defined up to multiples of $2\pi$.

atoms.title: Sequences and series
atoms.summary: A series is the limit of partial sums of a sequence; convergence tests decide when infinitely many terms add to a finite total, with absolute convergence being the well-behaved case.

depths.eli5: A 'sequence' is just a list of numbers in order. A 'series' is what you get when you add a sequence up. If you add infinitely many shrinking numbers, sometimes the running total settles on a finite answer (it 'converges') and sometimes it grows without bound (it 'diverges'). There are tests to tell which will happen. The cleanest example is the geometric series, where each term is a fixed fraction of the one before (like 1 + ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … = 2).
depths.core: A series Σaₙ converges if its 'partial sums' (the totals after 1 term, 2 terms, 3 terms, …) approach a limit. The geometric series 1 + r + r² + … sums to 1/(1−r) whenever |r| < 1. To decide trickier cases there are standard tools: the ratio and root tests compare a series to a geometric benchmark; the comparison and integral tests pin down others. A series 'converges absolutely' if Σ|aₙ| (the sum of the sizes) converges — and absolute convergence guarantees the total is unchanged no matter how you reorder the terms. 'Conditional' convergence (the series converges but Σ|aₙ| does not) gives no such guarantee.
depths.deep: Riemann's rearrangement theorem shows that a conditionally convergent series — the classic example is the alternating harmonic series 1 − ½ + ⅓ − ¼ + … — can be reshuffled to add up to ANY real number you like, or even to diverge. So infinite addition is not blindly commutative; order can matter. Power series (series in powers of x), which converge inside a disk in the complex plane, are the bridge connecting this topic to Taylor expansions and complex analysis.

atoms.note: The harmonic series 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ¼ + … diverges even though its terms shrink to zero — so terms going to zero is necessary but never enough to guarantee convergence.

quiz.answer: It sums to 1/(1−r) when |r|<1; for |r|≥1 the terms don't shrink to zero, so the series diverges.

quiz.prompt: Does Σ 1/n² converge, and what test settles it most cleanly?
quiz.answer: Yes — the integral test compares it to ∫1/x² dx, which is finite, so the series converges (in fact to π²/6).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
A **sequence** is a list of numbers in order; a **series** is what you get by adding them up. Add infinitely many shrinking numbers and sometimes the running total settles on a finite answer (it **converges**), sometimes it grows forever (**diverges**). The cleanest example is geometric: $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac18+\cdots=2$, where each term is a fixed fraction of the one before.

### Precisely
A series $\sum a_n$ **converges** if its partial sums $s_N=\sum_{n=0}^N a_n$ approach a limit. The **geometric series** sums to
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} r^n=\frac{1}{1-r}\quad(|r|<1).$$
To test trickier series there are the ratio, root, comparison, and integral tests. A series **converges absolutely** if $\sum|a_n|$ converges — and absolute convergence guarantees the sum is unchanged under any reordering. Merely **conditional** convergence ($\sum a_n$ converges but $\sum|a_n|$ does not) gives no such guarantee.

### Worked example
Derive the geometric sum. Let $s=1+r+r^2+\cdots+r^N$. Multiply by $r$: $rs=r+r^2+\cdots+r^{N+1}$. Subtract: $s-rs=1-r^{N+1}$, so $s=\dfrac{1-r^{N+1}}{1-r}$. If $|r|<1$ then $r^{N+1}\to0$ as $N\to\infty$, leaving $\dfrac{1}{1-r}$. For $r=\tfrac12$ this is $\dfrac{1}{1-1/2}=2$, matching $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\cdots=2$.

### Why it works
The "multiply and subtract" telescoping is what collapses the partial sum into a closed form; convergence then hinges entirely on whether $r^{N+1}$ dies, which happens exactly when $|r|<1$. For other series the standard tests compare against this geometric benchmark.

### Where it connects
Series rest on the `limit`. Power series (series in $x^n$) link to `taylor` and `complex-analysis`. Orthogonal-function series are `fourier` series. Convergence questions feed `real-analysis` (uniform convergence) and `recurrence-generating` functions.

### Watch out
**Terms shrinking to zero is necessary but not sufficient.** The harmonic series $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\cdots$ has terms going to $0$ yet diverges. And **order can matter**: Riemann's rearrangement theorem shows a conditionally convergent series like $1-\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\tfrac14+\cdots$ can be reshuffled to sum to *any* value you choose. Infinite addition is not blindly commutative.

atoms.title: Gradient, divergence, and curl
atoms.equation: \nabla f=\Big(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial x},\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial y},\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\Big)
atoms.summary: Multivariable calculus extends differentiation to fields: the gradient points uphill steepest, divergence measures outflow, and curl measures rotation.

depths.eli5: Imagine a hilly landscape. At any spot, the 'gradient' is the arrow pointing straight up the steepest slope, and its length tells you how steep. Now imagine a flowing fluid instead: 'divergence' tells you where fluid is spreading out (a source) or piling in (a sink), and 'curl' tells you where it is swirling like a little whirlpool.
depths.core: A 'partial derivative' measures how a multi-input function changes when you nudge just one input and hold the rest fixed. The gradient, written ∇f (the symbol ∇ is called 'nabla' or 'del'), bundles all the partial derivatives into a single vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase; it is always perpendicular to the 'level sets' (the contour lines of constant value). For a vector field F (an arrow attached to every point, like wind), the divergence ∇·F measures the net outflow per unit volume (sources and sinks), and the curl ∇×F measures the local spinning. These three operators, all built from ∇, organize the whole of vector calculus.
depths.deep: Identities such as curl(grad f) = 0 and div(curl F) = 0 are not accidents — they are the single statement d²=0 from the language of differential forms. They encode two facts: a 'conservative' field (one that is a gradient) has a potential and does no net work around a loop, and anything that purely circulates has no net source. This is the local, point-by-point face of the generalized Stokes' theorem.

atoms.note: The gradient is always perpendicular to the level set (contour) through a point — and that is exactly why it points in the direction of fastest increase.

quiz.prompt: What does the gradient of a scalar field point toward, and how does it relate to level sets?
quiz.answer: It points in the direction of steepest increase of the function, and it is always perpendicular to the level sets (contours) of that function.

quiz.prompt: Compute the gradient of f(x,y) = x²y at the point (1,2).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Imagine a hilly landscape. At any spot the **gradient** is the arrow pointing straight up the steepest slope, its length telling you how steep. Now imagine a flowing fluid: **divergence** marks where fluid spreads out (a source) or piles in (a sink), and **curl** marks where it swirls like a little whirlpool. These three operators extend differentiation from single numbers to whole fields.

### Precisely
A **partial derivative** $\partial f/\partial x$ measures how $f$ changes when only $x$ varies. The **gradient** bundles them:
$$\nabla f=\Big(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial x},\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial y},\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\Big),$$
a vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase, always perpendicular to the level sets. For a vector field $F$, the **divergence** $\nabla\cdot F$ measures net outflow per unit volume, and the **curl** $\nabla\times F$ measures local rotation. All three are built from the operator $\nabla$ ("del").

### Worked example
Compute $\nabla f$ for $f(x,y)=x^2y$ at the point $(1,2)$. The partials are $\partial f/\partial x=2xy$ and $\partial f/\partial y=x^2$. So $\nabla f=(2xy,\ x^2)$; at $(1,2)$ this is $(2\cdot1\cdot2,\ 1^2)=(4,1)$. This arrow points in the direction of fastest increase of $f$ at that point, and the value of $f$ rises most rapidly along $(4,1)$, perpendicular to the contour through $(1,2)$.

### Why it works
The gradient is perpendicular to level sets because moving *along* a contour keeps $f$ constant, so the directional derivative is zero there — and the directional derivative is $\nabla f$ dotted with the direction. It is zero exactly when the direction is orthogonal to $\nabla f$, so $\nabla f$ must point across the contours, i.e. uphill.

### Where it connects
This generalizes the `derivative` to fields and rests on `vector-space` structure. The gradient drives `optimization` (extrema where $\nabla f=0$). Identities like $\nabla\times(\nabla f)=0$ and $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times F)=0$ are the local face of the `stokes-theorem` and the seed of `manifolds`' $d^2=0$.

### Watch out
Existence of all partial derivatives does **not** by itself guarantee differentiability in the full sense — the function can still behave badly along diagonal directions. True differentiability requires the linear (gradient) approximation to have error vanishing faster than the step size, not merely that each partial exists.

atoms.title: Ordinary differential equations
atoms.summary: An ODE relates a function to its derivatives; solving one finds the function whose rate of change obeys a given law, with existence and uniqueness guaranteed under mild conditions.

depths.eli5: An ODE ('ordinary differential equation') is a rule that says how fast something is changing in terms of where it is right now. Solving the ODE means reconstructing the whole story over time from that rule — for example, knowing a population's growth rate at any size and using it to predict the population far into the future.
depths.core: A first-order ODE has the form y' = f(t,y), where y' is the rate of change: it prescribes the slope at every point in the plane, and a solution is a curve that always follows the local slope (it 'threads the slope field'). Linear ODEs with constant coefficients are solved by exponential functions e^(λt), where the allowed exponents λ are the roots of a 'characteristic polynomial' — the same eigenvalue idea from linear algebra. The Picard–Lindelöf theorem guarantees exactly one solution passing through each starting point, provided f is 'Lipschitz' in y (it does not change too abruptly).
depths.deep: A system of linear ODEs y' = Ay is solved by diagonalizing the matrix A: its eigenvalues set the growth/decay rates and oscillation frequencies, tying the behavior directly to A's spectrum. Nonlinear ODEs rarely have a clean formula solution, so mathematicians switch to qualitative methods (locating equilibrium 'fixed points', testing their stability, drawing 'phase portraits' of the flow) and to numerical simulation. Extreme sensitivity to starting conditions here is the doorway to chaos theory.

atoms.note: The exponential function is the 'eigenfunction' of differentiation — differentiating e^(λt) just multiplies it by λ — which is precisely why exponentials solve linear ODEs.

quiz.prompt: Solve y' = ky and state the role of the initial condition.
quiz.answer: y = y₀e^{kt}; the initial value y₀ = y(0) fixes the single constant of integration, selecting one curve from the family of solutions.

quiz.prompt: What does the Picard–Lindelöf theorem guarantee, and what condition does it need?
quiz.answer: A unique solution through each initial point, provided f(t,y) is continuous and Lipschitz continuous in y near that point.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
An **ordinary differential equation** (ODE) is a rule that says how fast something changes in terms of where it is right now. Solving it means reconstructing the entire history (and future) from that local rule — for instance, knowing a population's growth rate at any size and using it to predict the population far ahead. Differential equations are how the laws of nature are written.

### Precisely
A first-order ODE has the form
$$\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y),$$
prescribing the slope at every point; a **solution** is a curve threading that slope field. The simplest important case is $y'=ky$, solved by $y=y_0e^{kt}$ where $y_0=y(0)$ is the initial condition. The **Picard–Lindelöf theorem** guarantees a *unique* solution through each starting point provided $f$ is continuous and **Lipschitz** in $y$ (it does not change too abruptly).

### Worked example
Solve $y'=ky$ by separation of variables. Write $\dfrac{dy}{y}=k\,dt$ and integrate both sides: $\ln|y|=kt+C$. Exponentiate: $|y|=e^{C}e^{kt}$, so $y=Ae^{kt}$ for a constant $A$. Apply the initial condition $y(0)=y_0$: $A=y_0$. Hence $y=y_0e^{kt}$. For $k>0$ this is exponential growth; for $k<0$, decay (e.g. radioactive material with half-life set by $k$).

### Why it works
The exponential is the **eigenfunction of differentiation**: $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{kt}=k\,e^{kt}$, just multiplication by $k$. So an exponential automatically satisfies $y'=ky$. For linear systems $y'=Ay$, diagonalizing $A$ (its `eigenvalue`s) decouples the equations into independent exponential modes.

### Where it connects
ODEs build on the `derivative` and `integral`. Linear constant-coefficient ODEs share the **characteristic equation** idea with `recurrence-generating`. Systems tie directly to `eigenvalue`s and `linear-map`s. The `fourier` transform converts differentiation to multiplication, turning some ODEs into algebra.

### Watch out
Most **nonlinear** ODEs have no closed-form solution — you switch to qualitative analysis (equilibria, stability, phase portraits) or numerics. And uniqueness can fail without the Lipschitz condition: $y'=\sqrt{|y|}$ with $y(0)=0$ has *multiple* solutions, a warning that the existence-uniqueness hypotheses do real work.

atoms.title: Fourier series and transform
atoms.summary: Fourier analysis decomposes a function into pure frequencies; periodic signals become discrete series and general ones become a continuous spectrum, with the basis being orthogonal exponentials.

depths.eli5: Any signal — a sound, a radio wave, an image — can be broken into pure single-frequency tones, the way a prism splits white light into a rainbow of colors. The Fourier transform is that prism for signals: it tells you exactly how much of each frequency is mixed in. Add the tones back up and you rebuild the original signal.
depths.core: Over one period, the basic building blocks are the complex exponentials e^(2πinx) — and they are mutually 'orthogonal' (perpendicular in the inner-product sense), so they form an orthonormal basis. A periodic function is therefore a weighted sum of these building blocks, called its Fourier series, with each weight ('coefficient') obtained by an inner product. For a non-repeating function the sum turns into an integral — the Fourier transform — which maps the function to its 'frequency content' (the spectrum). A key payoff: differentiating a signal corresponds to simply multiplying its transform by the frequency, which converts hard differential equations into easy algebra.
depths.deep: Fourier analysis is the spectral theorem applied to the differentiation operator: the complex exponentials are its eigenfunctions. Plancherel's theorem says the transform preserves total energy (the L² norm), making it a 'unitary' (length-preserving) map. The uncertainty principle — a signal and its transform cannot both be sharply concentrated — is a genuine theorem here, of which the physics version in quantum mechanics is a special case.

atoms.note: Convolution (a smearing/blending operation) in one domain becomes plain multiplication in the other — the property that makes the Fourier transform the backbone of signal processing and of solving partial differential equations (PDEs).

quiz.prompt: What basis does a Fourier series expand a periodic function in, and why is orthogonality essential?
quiz.answer: The complex exponentials (equivalently sines and cosines); orthogonality lets each coefficient be extracted independently via an inner product, with no cross-contamination between frequencies.

quiz.prompt: Why does the Fourier transform simplify solving linear differential equations?
quiz.answer: It converts differentiation into multiplication by frequency (×2πiξ), turning a differential equation into an algebraic one in the frequency domain that you solve and transform back.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Any signal — a sound, a radio wave, an image — can be broken into pure single-frequency tones, the way a prism splits white light into a rainbow. The **Fourier transform** is that prism for signals: it reports exactly how much of each frequency is present. Add the tones back and you rebuild the original. This decomposition is one of the most useful ideas in all of applied mathematics.

### Precisely
On one period, the building blocks are the complex exponentials $e^{2\pi i n x}$, which are mutually **orthogonal** in the inner-product sense, hence an orthonormal basis. A periodic function is a weighted sum of them — its **Fourier series** — with each weight obtained by an inner product. For a non-periodic function the sum becomes an integral, the **Fourier transform**:
$$\hat f(\xi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx,$$
mapping $f$ to its frequency content $\hat f$.

### Worked example
Why does the transform simplify differential equations? Differentiate $f$ and transform: integration by parts shows $\widehat{f'}(\xi)=2\pi i\xi\,\hat f(\xi)$. So **differentiation becomes multiplication by $2\pi i\xi$**. A differential equation like $f''+f=g$ transforms into $\big((2\pi i\xi)^2+1\big)\hat f=\hat g$, an *algebraic* equation $\hat f=\dfrac{\hat g}{1-4\pi^2\xi^2}$. Solve for $\hat f$, then transform back. The hard calculus problem became simple division in the frequency domain.

### Why it works
Orthogonality of the exponentials is the crux: it lets each coefficient be extracted independently via an inner product, with no cross-contamination between frequencies. The exponentials are eigenfunctions of differentiation ($\tfrac{d}{dx}e^{2\pi i\xi x}=2\pi i\xi\,e^{2\pi i\xi x}$), which is why $d/dx$ turns into multiplication — Fourier analysis is the `spectral-theorem` for the derivative operator.

### Where it connects
It rests on `inner-product` (orthogonality), `sequences-series` (the series), and `complex-numbers` (Euler's exponentials). Convolution in one domain becomes multiplication in the other, the backbone of signal processing and solving PDEs. Energy is preserved (Plancherel's theorem), making the transform unitary.

### Watch out
The **uncertainty principle** is a genuine theorem here: a signal and its transform cannot both be sharply concentrated — narrow in time forces wide in frequency. (The quantum-mechanical version is a special case.) So you cannot have perfect time *and* frequency localization simultaneously.

atoms.title: Topological spaces
atoms.summary: Topology axiomatizes 'nearness' through open sets alone, abstracting away distance; it captures the properties of shape that survive continuous deformation, like connectedness and compactness.

depths.eli5: Topology is geometry without a ruler — it only cares about which points are 'near' each other, not how far apart they are. To a topologist a coffee mug and a donut are the same shape, because you could mold one into the other (the handle becomes the hole) without ever tearing or gluing. Stretching is allowed; cutting is not.
depths.core: A topology on a set is a chosen collection of subsets called 'open sets', required to include the whole space and the empty set and to stay closed under any unions and finite intersections. Remarkably, that alone is enough to define continuity (a map is continuous if the pre-image of every open set is open) — no notion of distance needed. The structure-preserving sameness here is 'homeomorphism' (a continuous deformation with a continuous inverse). Three big properties classify spaces: connectedness (cannot be split into two separate open pieces), compactness (every covering by open sets has a finite sub-covering), and the Hausdorff property (distinct points can be separated by disjoint opens).
depths.deep: Compactness is the topological distillation of 'closed and bounded': it is what guarantees a continuous function attains its maximum and otherwise behaves. The Heine–Borel theorem says compactness matches 'closed and bounded' exactly in finite-dimensional spaces (but not in infinite-dimensional ones). To actually tell spaces apart, topologists attach algebraic gadgets — the fundamental group (loops up to deformation) and homology — turning qualitative shape questions into computable algebra.

atoms.note: Every metric space is automatically a topological space (its distance defines the open sets), but not every topology comes from a distance — so topology is strictly more general than metric geometry.

quiz.prompt: How is continuity defined in topology without reference to distance?
quiz.answer: A map is continuous if the preimage of every open set is open; this recovers the metric notion of continuity using only the open-set structure.

quiz.prompt: What does compactness guarantee for a continuous real-valued function on a compact space?
quiz.answer: The function attains a maximum and minimum value (the extreme value theorem); its image is also compact, hence closed and bounded.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
**Topology** is geometry without a ruler — it cares only about which points are "near" each other, not how far apart. To a topologist a coffee mug and a donut are the *same* shape, because one can be molded into the other (the handle becomes the hole) without tearing or gluing. Stretching is allowed; cutting is not. Topology captures the properties of shape that survive continuous deformation.

### Precisely
A **topology** on a set $X$ is a collection $\tau$ of subsets called **open sets** such that $\emptyset,X\in\tau$, and $\tau$ is closed under **arbitrary unions** and **finite intersections**. Remarkably, that alone defines continuity: $f$ is continuous iff the preimage of every open set is open — no distance required. The right notion of sameness is **homeomorphism** (a continuous bijection with continuous inverse). Three structural properties: **connectedness** (not splittable into two separate opens), **compactness** (every open cover has a finite subcover), and **Hausdorff** (distinct points separable by disjoint opens).

### Worked example
What does compactness buy you? Consider a continuous real-valued function on a compact space. Its image is compact, hence (in $\mathbb{R}$) closed and bounded, so the function **attains a maximum and a minimum** — the extreme value theorem. Concretely, $f(x)=x$ on the *closed* interval $[0,1]$ attains its max $1$; but on the *open* interval $(0,1)$, which is not compact, $f$ has supremum $1$ that it never reaches. Compactness is exactly what rescues the existence of extremes.

### Why it works
Defining continuity through open sets generalizes the metric "preimage of small ball is small" while discarding the metric itself. Compactness is the topological distillation of "closed and bounded"; the Heine–Borel theorem confirms they coincide in finite-dimensional spaces (but not in infinite-dimensional ones).

### Where it connects
Every `metric-space` is automatically a topological space (its distance defines the opens), but not every topology comes from a distance — so topology is strictly more general. It is the home of `manifolds` and `complex-analysis`'s "simply connected" regions. To tell spaces apart, topologists attach algebra — the fundamental group, homology.

### Watch out
Topology is *coarser* than geometry: it cannot see length, angle, or curvature, only connectivity-type features. So a circle and a square are topologically identical (both homeomorphic to each other), even though geometrically they differ. Don't expect topological invariants to distinguish shapes that differ only by stretching.

atoms.title: Determinants
atoms.summary: The determinant is the signed volume-scaling factor of a linear map; it is zero exactly when the map collapses dimension, signaling non-invertibility.

depths.eli5: Push a unit square (or cube) through a transformation and look at the shape that comes out. atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Push a unit square (or cube) through a linear transformation and look at the output shape. The **determinant** is the area (or volume) of that output — with a minus sign if the transformation flipped the figure over like a mirror. If the determinant is zero, the shape got squashed completely flat: the transformation destroyed a dimension and cannot be undone.

### Precisely
The determinant is the unique function on square matrices that is **linear in each column**, **alternating** (swapping two columns flips its sign), and equals $1$ on the identity. Geometrically it is the signed volume-scaling factor of the map. It is **multiplicative**, and detects invertibility:
$$\det(AB)=\det A\,\det B,\qquad A^{-1}\ \text{exists}\iff\det A\ne0.$$
$\det A=0$ means the map is **singular** — it collapses some nonzero vector to zero, i.e. has a nontrivial kernel.

### Worked example
Compute $\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$. For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ the determinant is $ad-bc$. Here that is $1\cdot4-2\cdot3=4-6=-2$. Since $-2\ne0$, the matrix is invertible. The magnitude $2$ says the map doubles areas; the *negative sign* says it reverses orientation (it includes a reflection). The unit square of area $1$ becomes a parallelogram of area $2$, mirror-flipped.

### Why it works
The three defining properties force the formula. Alternating linearity means swapping equal columns gives both $+\det$ and $-\det$, so a matrix with two equal (or dependent) columns has determinant $0$ — capturing that dependent columns flatten space. Multiplicativity reflects that composing maps multiplies their volume factors.

### Where it connects
The determinant powers the characteristic polynomial $\det(A-\lambda I)$ and thus `eigenvalue`s; the Jacobian determinant rescaling volume in `change-of-variables`; and Cramer's rule for solving linear systems. Its **sign** tracks orientation — distinguishing rotations from reflections — the algebraic seed of orientation in geometry and `manifolds`.

### Watch out
$\det A=0$ is the precise signal of **non-invertibility** and **linear dependence** of columns — don't read a small nonzero determinant as "almost singular" in a naive way (that role belongs to the condition number / singular values in `svd`). Also, the determinant alone does not tell you *which* directions get collapsed; for that you need the kernel.

atoms.title: Completeness and uniform convergence
atoms.summary: Real analysis rigorizes calculus: completeness of ℝ makes limits exist, and uniform convergence is the condition that lets you swap limits with integrals and derivatives.

depths.eli5: Calculus works only because the real number line has no holes: any sequence of numbers that crowds together toward a value really does reach an actual number. 'Real analysis' is the careful study that makes calculus airtight. A second key idea: when a whole family of functions settles toward a limiting function evenly — at the same pace everywhere at once — you are allowed to integrate or differentiate the limit safely. If the settling is uneven, you can get wrong answers.
depths.core: Completeness — the property that every Cauchy sequence (terms huddling ever closer) actually converges to a point in the set — is what separates the reals ℝ from the rationals ℚ, and it guarantees that suprema (least upper bounds), limits, and integrals exist when they should. There are two notions of a sequence of functions converging to a limit: 'pointwise' (each input converges at its own pace) is too weak — the limit of the integrals can disagree with the integral of the limit — whereas 'uniform' convergence (a single rate works for every input simultaneously) lets you safely swap the limit with integration, and with care with differentiation. That control is exactly what distinguishes rigorous analysis from naive symbol-pushing.
depths.deep: The strange examples that forced mathematicians to be careful — Weierstrass's function that is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere, or a convergent series whose term-by-term derivative blows up — prove that intuition fails without uniform control. Heavier tools like the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem and the dominated convergence theorem allow swapping limits under weaker assumptions, and they lead naturally into measure theory.

atoms.note: A pointwise limit of continuous functions can be discontinuous, but a uniform limit of continuous functions is always continuous — uniformity is what preserves continuity.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition
Calculus works only because the real number line has **no holes**: any sequence of numbers crowding together toward a value really does reach an actual number. Real analysis is the careful study that makes calculus airtight. A second key idea: when a whole family of functions settles toward a limit *evenly* — at the same pace everywhere — you may safely integrate or differentiate the limit. Uneven settling can give wrong answers.

### Precisely
**Completeness** of $\mathbb{R}$ means every Cauchy sequence (terms with $|x_m-x_n|\to0$) converges to a point in $\mathbb{R}$; equivalently, every bounded set has a least upper bound. For a sequence of functions, **pointwise** convergence ($f_n(x)\to f(x)$ at each $x$, each at its own rate) is too weak, whereas **uniform** convergence (one rate works for all $x$ at once) lets you swap the limit with the integral:
$$f_n\to f\ \text{uniformly}\ \Rightarrow\ \lim_n\int f_n=\int f.$$

### Worked example
Pointwise is not enough. Let $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$. Pointwise it converges to $f$ with $f(x)=0$ for $x<1$ and $f(1)=1$ — a *discontinuous* limit of continuous functions, and the convergence is not uniform near $x=1$. Now a sharper warning: there exist sequences $f_n$ with $\int_0^1 f_n=1$ for all $n$ yet $f_n\to0$ pointwise, so $\lim\int f_n=1\ne0=\int\lim f_n$. Only *uniform* convergence forbids such mismatches.

### Why it works
A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous because a single $\delta$ controls every $f_n$ simultaneously, so continuity passes to the limit. Completeness guarantees the limits, suprema, and integrals we expect actually exist — in $\mathbb{Q}$ they can fail (a Cauchy sequence approaching $\sqrt2$ converges to nothing rational).

### Where it connects
It rigorizes the `limit`, `derivative`, `integral`, and `sequences-series`, and rests on `metric-space` completeness. Pathological examples (Weierstrass's everywhere-continuous nowhere-differentiable function) motivate `measure-theory`, whose dominated convergence theorem swaps limits under weaker hypotheses.

### Watch out
**Pointwise convergence preserves almost nothing** — not continuity, not the value of integrals or derivatives. Always check for *uniform* convergence (or a domination hypothesis) before interchanging a limit with an integral or derivative. Naive symbol-swapping is exactly the trap real analysis exists to prevent.

atoms.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
atoms.summary: Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root; equivalently ℂ is algebraically closed, so every degree-n polynomial factors into n linear pieces.

depths.eli5: Once you allow complex numbers (the system that includes i, the square root of −1), every polynomial equation has a solution — there are no 'unsolvable' ones left. And a degree-n polynomial doesn't just have one root; it splits completely into n simple linear pieces.
depths.core: The theorem says the complex numbers ℂ are 'algebraically closed': any polynomial of degree at least 1 with complex coefficients has at least one root in ℂ. Pull that root out as a factor, repeat, and you find the polynomial factors completely into linear pieces — counted with multiplicity, exactly n of them for degree n. This is why ℂ, not the reals ℝ, is the natural home of algebra: the hunt for roots that began with inventing √−1 finally ends here, with nothing more to add.
depths.deep: Strikingly, every known proof leans on analysis or topology — no purely algebraic argument suffices, because the statement is ultimately about ℂ's continuous, gap-free (topological) structure. The slickest proof uses Liouville's theorem (any bounded function that is complex-differentiable everywhere must be constant): if a polynomial p had no root, then 1/p would be bounded and complex-differentiable everywhere, hence constant — contradicting that p has positive degree. So p must have a root. The result is a keystone linking algebra, analysis, and topology.

atoms.note: It guarantees the roots EXIST; it does not give a formula for them. Galois theory shows that degree-5-and-higher polynomials generally have no solution 'by radicals' (using only +, −, ×, ÷, and nth roots), even though their roots provably exist.
